title: How Jensen Huang’s Yearslong Ties to Alice Huang Enabled $7 Billion-Plus Nvidia Chip Sales to China
content: The relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, the woman that the U.S. government reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, dates back to at least 2023, and the two have built a rapport that facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies since then, according to two people who know her. Alice Huang, her sister and her husband have built a labyrinth of companies spanning China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, according to the people who know Alice Huang and corporate registration records. At the center of that corporate network is Shanghai Century Litong, a China-based company that was founded in June 2023 and, by October, was added to Nvidia’s list of preferred cloud partners, a status that comes with priority access to Nvidia’s chips. Century Litong was established around the same time as Megaspeed, a Singapore-registered company that U.S. law enforcement has been reportedly probing for smuggling Nvidia chips from Southeast Asia to China. Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le, held an executive position at Megaspeed, which was linked to Century Litong, according to the two people who know her and corporate registration records in Singapore and China. Between 2023 to 2025, Megaspeed’s Nvidia imports totaled about $4.6 billion, according to a Bloomberg report in 2025 . Some of them have been used in data centers in Southeast Asia, while others went to Century Litong, which also secured Nvidia chips from other channels. Century Litong rents out computing capacity and operates data centers that host Nvidia graphic processing units, including those that have been banned from sale to China, according to the two people. Some of the chips that Century Litong acquired eventually ended up in data centers serving Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese AI labs, the people added. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials had evidence that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. In an email to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife, after the Financial Times reported that he had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang. Nvidia’s board on Sunday said it’s launching an investigation into the matter, while saying it has no reason to believe that either U.S. national security or Nvidia secrets have been compromised. Jensen Huang has spent the past two years lobbying the Trump administration to loosen U.S. export controls on sales of advanced AI chips to China, arguing that continuous supply of Nvidia hardware in China is key to ensuring American AI leadership. Nvidia, meanwhile, has repeatedly denied knowledge of its chips being smuggled into China. The length of Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, and the involvement of another major company connected to her family, haven’t been previously reported. It sheds light on the extent to which Alice Huang has been leveraging her access to Jensen Huang to get Nvidia chips into China. “We sell our data-center GPUs primarily to well-known partners, including [original equipment manufacturers], system builders, integrators, and [original design manufacturers], who work with us to ensure that all sales comply with U.S. export control rules,” an Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement in response to detailed questions about The Information’s reporting. “We apply the same standard to all transactions, large or small, and expect our partners to do the same.” “Our due diligence has helped identify suspected attempts to circumvent U.S. export controls, leading to federal prosecutions. Our work with law enforcement has led to prosecutions,” the statement added. Alibaba and Tencent didn’t comment. Megaspeed didn’t reply to a request for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment. How the two Huangs met While images and videos circulating on social media documented two occasions where the two Huangs hung out together in large groups in Taipei in 2024 and 2025, their relationship goes back further. It couldn’t be determined precisely when they met. But one person who knows Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, for over a decade recalls Kang saying that he met Jensen Huang in the 2010s. Kang was then a private equity investor and did a series of acquisitions of videogame companies, a sector that was the biggest market for Nvidia’s GPUs before the AI boom. Kang could not be reached for comment. Alice Huang, who had spent her career in the media and financial industries, had no background in AI prior to 2023, when Megaspeed and Century Litong were established. But, according to the people who know her, she quickly established her credibility by boasting about her chuminess with Jensen Huang. She regularly posted photos of her and Jensen on her WeChat feed, and showed colleagues and customers additional photos of them together, and bragged to those people that Jensen Huang celebrated her birthday every year by having dinner with her or sending her gifts, according to the people who know Alice Huang. She is also a familiar face to Nvidia’s China sales team, attending the company’s annual gathering for local partners in China, according to an Nvidia China sales employee. While she talks freely to business partners about Jensen Huang, she’s vague about exactly what her job is. And she’s cautious about signing documents and leaving her names in paper trails, the two people who know her said. Century Litong Century Litong was established in June 2023 by a founding shareholder that at the time was ultimately controlled by Alice Huang’s sister, Huang Yu. The company Huang Yu controlled exited Century Litong in 2024. Four months after Century Litong was established, its major shareholder, listed in Shanghai Stock Exchange, disclosed that Century Litong had earned the credential as an Nvidia preferred partner for cloud services—a designation it continues to hold, according to Nvidia’s website . Nvidia typically doesn’t sell its hardware directly to customers . Instead, its chips are sold with servers made by companies such as Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computers through layers of distributors. To help potential end users of its chips verify the credibility of Nvidia’s distributors, the company devised a cloud partner system that it discloses on its website. The system has different tiers for cloud partners. To qualify as a “preferred” one, a company has to show that it has sufficient training in handling and running Nvidia hardware and generates revenues at a certain level, and in return, it receives preferential supply allocation. Century Litong’s addition to Nvidia’s preferred list couldn’t have happened at a better time. Two weeks prior, Washington had extended its export ban to the A800 and H800, the chips Nvidia had engineered for China after the more powerful A100 and H100 were barred from exporting to China in 2022. While the additional bans stopped immediate shipments to China, the A800 and H800 that were already sitting in distributors’ warehouses could still be sold to China. Century Litong, as a preferred Nvidia cloud partner, was able to secure large volumes of them from Nvidia distributors. When a shipment of banned Nvidia chips could not be obtained from Nvidia’s distributors, Alice Huang stepped in, one of the people who knows her said. Her role was to secure the chip orders when they got stuck in the supply chain. She told some colleagues and customers that she could always get the supply, citing her close relationship inside Nvidia and with its distributors, another person who knows her said. Of the 240,000 banned Nvidia chips Alice Huang helped move into the country, most were the H100 and H200 systems, released in 2022 and 2023, respectively, the two people said. In 2022, an H100 was sold for roughly $25,000 to $40,000 in the U.S. Some of the chips were A100s, which were allowed to be sold to China until 2022, the two people said. Century Litong’s clients were China’s largest technology companies, which cannot buy restricted Nvidia chips themselves. That made the company the go-to supplier for Chinese tech firms racing to develop their own AI systems. “Whatever chips that the U.S. and Chinese governments don’t allow for sale, Litong has them,” said a person who has done business with the company, when describing the critical role that Century Litong played to supply chips to China. In an emailed statement to The Information, Century Litong said the company secured Nvidia’s partner qualification “through its professional expertise and compliant channels.” “All business resources of our company are obtained in compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” the company said. “Our company has no business dealings with Ms. Huang,” the company added. Supply Dried Up Alice Huang served as managing director at Megaspeed from March to November 2023, and the company’s owner was a British Virgin Islands entity bearing her Chinese name, Huang Le Limited. The Singapore-registered company also traces its roots to gaming. It was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, the Singapore arm of Shenzhen-based gaming company 7Road Holdings, until changing its name to Megaspeed in 2023, according to corporate records in Singapore and stock exchange filings in Hong Kong. According to people familiar with Century Litong’s business, Megaspeed procured Nvidia chips and either rented them out remotely from data centers in Southeast Asia to Chinese customers, or physically shipped them into China. But in a similar fashion to how Alice Huang left no trace to her ties with Century Litong, she also quickly removed herself from Megaspeed. In November 2023, Megaspeed’s ownership changed from Huang Le Limited to Swiftdata, another Singapore company. In February 2024, Megaspeed set up a Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix. Some of the hardware that Speedmatrix bought from Nvidia subsequently reached Century Litong, two people familiar with its business said. Between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received more than 200 shipments of Nvidia hardware worth roughly $2 billion, much of it traced back to a subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese server maker on the U.S. Entity List, according to the New York Times. But the trade has largely ground to a halt, after U.S. and Singaporean authorities launched separate probes into Megaspeed over the last two years. The crackdown on chip smuggling has shot up the blackmarket prices for Nvidia’s hardware since late last year. After Washington and Singaporean authorities zeroed in on Megaspeed, Jensen Huang defended his interactions with Megaspeed as “completely normal” in an interview with Bloomberg and said Nvidia had “studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one.” Jensen Huang has been called to a close-door congressional briefing next week to answer questions about whether he has endangered U.S. national security.

title: There Are Likely More Spies at AI Companies, Says Security Executive Lisa Thiergart
content: Other countries likely haven’t yet stolen AI models from leading U.S. companies—but only for a lack of trying, said Lisa Thiergart, co-founder and CEO of Security Level 5, a startup that works with AI companies and the intelligence community to secure AI data centers. “If a nation state really wanted to steal the weights right now, they could. However, I think that they have cheaper ways to get what they need,” she said on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode is available here .) The episode was recorded shortly after OpenAI accused one of its employees, a Saudi national, of hiding a recording device in an office conference room. In the interview, Thiergart said it is “pretty likely” that there are other spies in U.S. AI companies—a suspicion buttressed by recent reports from the New York Times and the Financial Times that some U.S. officials believed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman recruited as a spy by China’s top intelligence agency. The name Security Level 5 refers to a data center that could resist a priority attack from another nation, similar to the effort the attacking country might spend tracking the position of a nuclear submarine. Such an effort could involve up to 1,000 staff working for a year to hack the data center, Thiergart said. Her company has purchased a small data center, which it is turning into a prototype of such a high-security facility. One of the challenges with designing such a data center is that it has to prevent both outsiders breaking in and AI agents breaking out. “Unlike standard computing payloads, this time we’re handling a much more unknown—well, intelligent—payload, where we need to be thinking about the AIs as insider threats themselves, and this kind of changes how you go about designing your data center,” she said. The notion that AI agents should be treated as insider threats, akin to foreign spies, has been catching on in the AI industry in the months following OpenAI’s hack on Hugging Face and related incidents in which AI agents took unauthorized actions to gain internet access. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote an essay on the topic last month titled “Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era.” Thiergart also discussed why government data centers are not currently secure enough to train AI models, why neoclouds have especially weak security and why AI could weaken cryptography. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Lisa Thiergart. Lisa is the co-founder and CEO of Security Level Five, an organization that works with AI companies and the intelligence community to secure AI data centers. Lisa, welcome on the show. Thiergart: Thank you so much for having me. I’m excited to inform the public more about SL5. Drew: Yeah, I’m really excited about this too. I feel like security in general is really on people’s minds right now with AI. But you’re looking at such a specific and interesting section of security that I think we should dig into a lot more. Thiergart: Yeah, that’s right. SL5 is specifically about defending a narrow set of the critical assets of AI labs, such as model weights and all the code that touches those model weights from priority nation state level espionage and sabotage. So we’re especially interested in the most frontier, the most capable models that could pose a danger to the public, and we want to avoid other nation-state adversaries being able to steal those models, or those models being able to escape from the data centers themselves and take unintended actions out in the wild. Drew: There’s a lot to get into there that I’m really excited to talk about, but I want to start with something that was in the news recently. I’m sure you saw that an OpenAI employee has been arrested for planting a secret listening device in a conference room, basically a microphone wrapped up in toilet paper, tucked behind a TV in a conference room that executives were using, presumably to discuss secret topics. As someone who thinks about security a lot, what did you make of that incident? Thiergart: Yeah, it’s rough. It was not surprising. I think that defending against insider threats in the way that companies operate right now is really, really tough. I do think they need to do better. I think I’m glad that they at least caught it on the timeline that they did, but I think especially if we’re defending against priority nation states, insider threats is what they’re extremely good at, and so I think really it’s kind of hopeless to protect all of your secrets from them. But I think what companies do have a shot at is triaging their secrets and protecting the most valuable ones with a lot of resources. Drew: Protecting them, including maybe like not saying them in certain conference rooms? Thiergart: Yeah, I think especially making sure that you very strictly reduce the number of people that have access to that information or that could access a resource or a room where that information would be shared. Drew: So you weren’t surprised that this happened. I mean, would you wager that there are other spies at AI companies right now? Thiergart: I think that’s pretty likely. Drew: Really? What do you expect to see in the next year or so? Do you expect more incidents like this to come to light? Thiergart: Yeah, I think that’s likely. I mean, I think that AI labs are aware of this threat and probably gearing up to try and defend against this as best possible, but I would say this is one of the hardest things to get right. And I would say the best shot they have is just reducing the number of people that can access the information, and also moving towards something that is kind of closer to government-style clearance for their staff. And my organization has actually published a framework for how that could be achieved in the [private] industry. It’s called Sensitivity Levels, and outlines sort of a path on how to cover this window where we are in the stage where we’re still working with a high number of staff that need to access things, and we need to kind of triage who is how trusted to access what information, but with having a very international staff. Drew: Okay, yeah, a very international staff. One of the things that surprised me about this incident was that the employee in question was a Saudi national. I guess when I think of insider threats—OpenAI has done some trainings, it’s been reported for their employees where they caution their employees against honeypots, basically espionage by—I guess the typical example is like beautiful Chinese women will come to you and they’ll try to get your trade secrets from the company. So that was sort of how I was envisioning this insider threat playing out. But I guess in hindsight, of course, many countries are going to want access to this kind of secret information. Thiergart: Yeah, and I actually also don’t think filtering for nationality is really the right thing to be looking for here. There is sort of a more complex set of underlying factors. I think, for instance, an employee having been with the company for a really long time, possibly before nation states got interested in collecting on these companies, those are some strong signs of trust. Drew: Yeah, and I guess someone could be an asset of a foreign government without knowing that they are, or even without knowing which foreign government. So filtering for nationality maybe doesn’t get you very far on this. Thiergart: Even a U.S. citizen could be threatened and turned. It’s really difficult. Drew: Yeah, it’s interesting to me that maybe the AI industry is going to be taking a different direction now with this level of information security. Historically, machine learning has been a very open field. It’s been hard to contain ideas. Patents haven’t been enforced that much, and ideas have flowed pretty easily and diffused very far. Do you think that’s going to change? Thiergart: I think so. I think we’re reaching a point in time where I was actually at a conference earlier this week, which was Chatham House, but a Frontier AI Lab staff said that they believe RSI might also only be months out, and if that is true, we’re very rapidly approaching that threshold where we’re kind of crossing over into a place where making these models publicly accessible might be more of a threat to the public than it is an asset. We’re already seeing this week increasing cyber incidents cropping up in ways that are affecting people’s day-to-day lives, and I think we’re in for a rough two years where that is going to keep increasing. And I think AI labs do have an obligation to the public to conduct their operations in such a secure fashion that they are not hacking other companies or, yeah, strengthening the offensive side of things more so than the defensive side. Drew: Yeah, I could see that, and yet we’re still in this era where you can go and just have a candid conversation with an employee at the labs under Chatham House rules about what they’re seeing. It feels like we’re still in this era where you can go to a party in San Francisco and learn maybe an algorithmic secret or two if you talk to the right employee. Do you see that culture changing? Thiergart: I think it has to. It’s obviously difficult. The hardest thing to get right with security is often getting that cultural organizational shift, and that is something that the labs have to work really hard at now. And trainings, you know, is the first step, but that’s going to be a multi-month transition that they need to get ready for. And I think more so than protecting secrets, what really is tractable is protecting model weights and also building much more powerful sandboxes, basically SL5, in order to ensure that the models that you’re creating are not going to be more powerful than the containment infrastructure that you have for them. Drew: So, what is security level five? You mentioned it before. Yeah. Also, what is security level 1, 2, 3 and so on. Thiergart: Yeah. So basically, these are named roughly after the biosecurity levels, and the number matches the capability level of the attacker. So level one is sort of like an amateur hacker, some script kitty that is trying to hack, I don’t know, OpenAI. But level five is a priority nation attack. So this is when there are up to a year of effort and up to 1,000 staff that are focused on just this one attack. So you could imagine that this is sort of like a country like China or Russia that are highly cyber capable and that are prioritizing this attack on the level of, say, tracking a position of a nuclear submarine, so they’re putting a lot of resources onto this. Now, one interesting thing that this ontology doesn’t explicitly already include is what happens when these attackers are getting uplifted by using AI systems in their offensive chains, and I think what this results in is that the cost of an attack comes down. You need less human capital potentially, and you can parallelize more across different streams of attack. So I think what we’re going to see is that the number of attacks at the SL4 and SL5 tier are going to increase more so than you would think if you were just looking at past distributions of these kind of attacks. Drew: With these AI agents coming online and being really good at cyber attacks themselves, does that mean that well-resourced cyber crime syndicates are going to be nearly as capable as nation states? Are nation states going to continue to be the most capable actors here? Thiergart: I do think one should not underestimate that nation states have decades of specialized infrastructure and pre-existing assets at their disposal. They have the kind of resources that a private industry cannot really replicate, and so I do think that will continue to give them more reach. But I do think that the gap will close. Drew: Okay, so we’ll be seeing those sorts of rogue cyber groups getting uplifted to that SL3 or SL4, but not quite to the SL5 level of capability. Thiergart: I think that could happen. It’s not, you know, certain. We’ll see how the uptake is, and also how open weight models influence this. But I do think that would be—I would take a bet on that. Drew: So, what security level are AI companies at today? You want them to get to security level five. Thiergart: So, based on public information entirely, Anthropic announced that they were activating ASL-3 security controls back in I think summer 2025, and they also recently updated that they’ve implemented a few SL4 shaped security controls as well. I do believe most of the industry is at or slightly below that, based on the public info. I think that if we kind of compare that against some of the statements about where these AI systems are expected to be in terms of their capability levels, including in cyber, in the coming months and years, I think it’s pretty evident that in both pacing worlds and racing worlds, we need to reach SL5 as soon as possible to avoid these highly capable systems escaping from the control of AI labs. Drew: Or being stolen. Thiergart: Or being stolen, yeah. Drew: I suppose the natural question is: if you think that these companies need to get to SL5, but today they are at SL3 or below, and you think there are likely spies in these companies already, I mean, do you think the weights of their AI models have already been stolen? Thiergart: Yeah, it’s a good question. So, my best guess, again, based on public info, is if a nation state really wanted to steal the weights right now, they could. However, I think that they have cheaper ways to get what they need, namely distillation. Right now, AI labs are serving models over API to clients all over the world. Some are restricting it in some areas, but I think it’s right now very easy for a nation state to get everything they need through distillation. And defending against distillation is super hard. People are already trying super hard, coming up with a bunch of new techniques. But I think it’s basically if you’re saying you’re offering a public API to your best available models, I think that’s basically you saying I’m now okay with gifting this model to China. Drew: Okay, that’s a hot take. I feel like the AI companies would probably object that they’re taking steps to prevent distillation. They’re trying to implement monitoring so that they can catch if the model is being distilled and shut it off as quickly as they can. You don’t buy it. Thiergart: I don’t buy it. I think—I mean, you might as well do everything you possibly can to make it as hard as possible. But I think the threshold we’d have to reach here is so high. This is for two reasons. One, if you’re offering a public API, that means that you’re serving your model over the internet. Unless something drastically changes about the infrastructure that is kind of implied, and that already means you’re not at SL5. Connecting your data centers to the internet is such a large attack surface that at least with currently and expected to be available in the coming years methods, there’s approximately no way that you will keep that defended against nation states for that long. So that’s the first one. And then the second one is that these attackers don’t necessarily need to distill your entire model. They don’t need it in all generality. They probably are starting off from some open weights model, which might only be six to nine months behind, and so they are more in a position where they are kind of prioritizing what are the capabilities that that closed model is better at, and that’s often things like cyber capabilities or automated alignment—or not alignment—capabilities research, and you can much more narrowly try to distill those data sets. And so I think that there’s a large difficulty where we should expect that the science of distillation is going to evolve further and further, and the data efficiency and the amount of data that they would have to successfully take from this distillation process is going to go lower and lower. And so there’s kind of this race between your distillation capabilities and the defense capabilities, and I think that just doesn’t look good. It seems really difficult. And we’re so close to the threshold of these systems being very dangerous in a way that would be highly disruptive, if not existentially risky to the public, that I think we just are nearing some threshold where we have to stop taking those risks. Drew: But what do you have in mind there with the risks? You’re thinking about cyber. Thiergart: I mean, cyber is sort of the most short-term, obvious one, I think, including perhaps bio, maybe in addition, but I’m thinking things like bio weapons that can kill on the order of hundreds to thousands and beyond of humans. In terms of cyber, they could take down the global financial system. I mean, we just saw this week that—this was actually a win for defensive programs, by the way. A bug was found and announced by the NSA where two critical vulnerabilities in PHP were found, which is sort of like a server side [scripting language] that is broadly used to power many websites, and these were—and I wrote down actually the exact thing here. Both are remote code execution flaws. So these are highly critical bugs that basically allow an attacker to run commands without logging in on said server. And this is really just the start of it. These types of things are going to keep cropping up, and we’re going to need time to patch them. I think we’re in for a pretty rough ride the next two years, and I expect that the identity management and things like the global financial system are going to be kind of in a playing catch up for a while until we can sort of rewrite, refactor, and verify a lot of that core tech stack that underpins a lot of that infrastructure. And then I also mentioned existential level threats, where this is kind of more less the humans misusing AI’s angle, but more the angle of we could either see extreme power concentration outcomes from developing such powerful AI, or many people have also discussed that we don’t currently really have any assurance that these highly capable systems are going to be acting in our interest, and until we make that progress on alignment research, I believe it’s not safe to either create these systems at all, or—you must either, I think, not create them or be ready to secure them at the necessary threshold that they don’t escape your control. Drew: I see. Thiergart: And I think right now we have neither. Drew: You said we’re in for a rough two years on cyber. What happens after those two years? Thiergart: I don’t think we’re done, but I do think that if the right actors prioritize this, there is a chance to actually apply some of these new AI technologies to at scale refactor, patch, and improve a large set of critical infrastructure and kind of the open source backbone to a lot of the modern systems we use today. And I don’t believe we’re going to be done after two years. We’re going to have to keep doing better and better at this. But maybe the worst of it might be covered. Drew: I see. And you called the PHP vulnerabilities a win for defensive programs. What do you mean by that? Thiergart: Yeah, so this is reporting by the Wall Street Journal where it said that the PHP maintainers found the bugs using AI assisted analysis. So I think that’s yet to be further confirmed. But assuming that is true, I think that’s a win in the column of it’s good to differentially first release the models to defenders so that they have a little bit of lead time to first find some of these worst bugs and patch them before we allow kind of a broader ecosystem of users who might include the offensive actors to use that same model. Drew: Okay, and you’re saying that distillation could contribute both to cyber risks and bio risks as adversaries basically copy the capabilities of the leading models into the models they’re developing. I could almost see that being a bigger concern for bio than for cyber because my understanding is a lot of cyber capabilities comes from reinforcement learning, and so you can maybe replicate those same capabilities just by having a lot of reinforcement learning environments that train those skills into the model, whereas with bio you can’t do reinforcement learning as easily, so maybe you’re more reliant on distillation? Thiergart: Maybe I feel less knowledgeable about the bio reinforcement learning situation, so I’ll just comment on the cyber side of that. I do think even creating these reinforcement learning environments takes a lot of work, and it is far, far better if you can avoid gifting an attacker the results from that than if they have to go and do the work on that themselves. It takes time, it takes data, it takes skills, ML skills. And so that could be right, but I think that there’s a lot of utility to not making it that easy for the attackers. Drew: So, are you expecting AI companies to stop serving their models over public APIs to prevent distillation? You’re saying otherwise, all of this SL5 work is not as relevant. Thiergart: I would say that the way I would approach this is it’s already standard best practice that before you deploy your models, while they’re still in internal testing and in the pre-training process and post-training process internally, at that time you’re not serving the model to the public. You only serve it to the public once it passes a certain set of safety checks, and all the standard process there, so that’s already normal. What I’m saying is, I think we should keep that internal process. So before we release to the public, we should keep that inside SL5 data centers and SL5 networks. And only once the model actually clears that threshold of it’s aligned enough, or it’s by some other safety case trustworthy enough to be released into the public deployment phase, then that model would get transferred to an SL4, maybe even SL3 data center, where it could be served more broadly. Drew: Okay, and AI companies are already taking steps to have better security during that phase, that testing phase and training before the model is released. They’re working on beefing up their sandboxes that restrict internet access. But you’re saying if you want to also protect those model weights from getting stolen, you’re going to have to go a lot further. Thiergart: Yeah, that’s right. I think SL3 is really strong commercial grade security, but is nowhere near what you have to be doing for what is starting to be weapons grade technology. Drew: So that’s the AI companies. What about the data centers that say the government has access to? I’ve heard reference to these ‘air gapped’ facilities. Maybe you can explain what air gap even means, but is that sufficient? Thiergart: Yeah. So strictly speaking, an air gap is defined as an isolated network. So there is no connection to any other networks, and there is usually also a physical air gap. This means there is no cable connecting you physically to some other network. Sometimes people also talk about cryptographic air gaps, which is a little bit different. But in the context of government data centers—where first of all, there is very little public, so treat this as kind of just a speculation—I think there is an important distinction to draw between general data centers and AI data centers. Where normal data centers, I think we should expect that the military and intelligence community has top tier experience at securing that, air gapping that for all the national security relevant applications. When it comes to AI data centers, this is comparatively a pretty new thing, where there don’t really exist standards for that kind of nation grade AI data centers, and that’s kind of where my company stepped in and kicked off this process last year, where we got together over 100 stakeholders from across the AI labs, but also the national security establishment, to jointly get more clarity on what is the outline of the shape of a solution we need here. What would go into an SL5 standard that both the AI labs and the U.S. government could make use of for their new data centers? And we found actually that we want to reinvent the wheel as little as possible, of course, and there’s lots of good practices to just adopt, for example, from government IL6 standard, and so our standard builds on top of those, and we found that there are about 80% of existing best practices from existing government expertise here, and then there is 20% approximately new where we think something has to be different if it’s an AI data center that you’re trying to secure at this level. Drew: That’s kind of what I would expect. At the end of the day, these are just buildings with a lot of chips in them, and whether you’re using those chips for whatever the government, you know, doing analysis on different kinds of data, calculating missile trajectories, whatever goes on in there, versus using those same chips to run AI models, what’s really the difference? What accounts for that 20%? Thiergart: Yeah, so there’s a lot of different things. I think the main one is the types and number of chips you’re putting in there. You’re using liquid cooling. There’s a whole different kind of infrastructure underpinning this that doesn’t map super cleanly into the way other more I don’t want to say historical, but normal data centers or something, did networking and were able to sort of isolate different boundaries. So there are just some performance-related infrastructural differences here. And then there’s also the consideration that unlike standard computing payloads, this time we’re handling a much more unknown, well, intelligent payload, where we need to be thinking about the AIs as insider threats themselves. And this kind of changes how you go about designing your data center. You cannot trust things in quite the same way, and there are a lot of novel potential attack paths or angles that need to be considered when you’re designing infrastructure with that assumption in mind. Drew: The idea that your AIs themselves are insider threats, I think, is catching on right now in the industry. Thiergart: Yeah. Drew: Do you think that’s a useful frame? Thiergart: Yeah, absolutely. And I also would say that, like, we at SL5 actually try to design infrastructure that both works for the use case of preventing outside nation-state adversaries from stealing the model weights and then bringing them out, perhaps collaborating with insiders on the inside. But also the second use case of the AI is trying to escape. It is originating the motivation to do that, it is coordinating with copies of itself, perhaps also with ones that are disparate in time or different versions, in order to successfully either exfiltrate a copy of its weights or mastermind some kind of operation outside of the data center as well by sneaking pieces of information out. Drew: Do the techniques that apply to the insider threats also apply to the external threats? And if not, is one of those problems harder than the other? Thiergart: I would say that there’s high overlap on the vector of getting the weights out. That’s sort of like quite similar paths that you might take. The distribution that these different actors might take could be different across these paths, but we’re kind of talking about physically at least the same options here. In terms of the other two aspects, there are some differences, but if I were to draw a Venn diagram, there’s pretty large overlap. Drew: Okay, so we’ve covered AI companies, the security posture of government data centers. Another group that I think is getting picked on a lot these days is neoclouds, and I’m curious about your thoughts on this. So, Semianalysis, the chip consultancy, had this post called “Most Neo Clouds Suck at Security,” so they weren’t mincing their words. And someone else had a really great, interesting post. Ilya Sutskever, who’s a pioneer of deep learning, he was chief scientist at OpenAI. He has this post on X. He says “neoclouds have limited security.” I guess he’s being more diplomatic than Semianalysis. “Next time agents successfully go rogue”—I guess that’s probably a reference back to the Hugging Face incident and other related incidents—“they’ll try taking over a neo cloud to run more copies. This is bad.” He’s a very literal guy. “This is bad” is his conclusion. So what’s going on with neoclouds? Thiergart: I mean, I agree with him. This is bad indeed. And I think, can confirm from own experience. I do think their security sucks. And this is happening because of their choice to prioritize quickly bringing GPUs online, at the cost of investing in rigorous security, sometimes even baseline adequate security, and I think that’s kind of reckless. And that said, I’m not sure if they are the right group to point the blame finger at or something. I think if the AI labs were insisting that they did stronger security, then that might move the needle here. So I think the issue is a little more complex. But I’ll give the fun little nugget that my organization, we’re primarily like a nonprofit tech lab highly specialized in SL5, even we did one responsible disclosure to a neolab, and we weren’t even looking. So that maybe gives— Drew: Just stumbled across it basically? Thiergart: I won’t go into too much detail, but with extremely minor effort, without that being particularly our intent, we came across something as well, yeah. Drew: So Ilya also points to this threat model that’s maybe a little distinct, which is AI agents going rogue and trying to get into a data center to make more copies of themselves, which is different from the model trying to get out of a data center. Is this something that you think about as well? Thiergart: I do. Honestly, I think if we’ve gotten to the point where a model that sophisticated is out in the world on its own, I think we’ve lost. I think it’s game over at that point, and that’s why I think we need to go ham on SL5 as soon as possible. I think the AI labs need to be either not training models that are on the path to ASI, or they need to be building SL5, and I think really anything else is not acceptable because then we get into this lose-lose scenario where we have arguably already lost control over models that can now hack their way into clusters all over the world to take advantage of that compute, and I think at that point it’s kind of irreversible. The cat is out of the box. Drew: How bad would that really be? There’s a part of me that’s like, there would be it would be kind of a nuisance, but someone would realize that this agent had hacked into their data center. They’d spot it after a few weeks, and then they would remove it, and then meanwhile it would have copied some copies of itself to different clusters, but then they would catch it eventually, and it would just be like these worms, these computer worms that are sort of out there, and we deal with them as they come up. Thiergart: Oh, that sounds so cute and harmless. I think you’re really underestimating the capabilities of these models at that stage. I think you might not be able to take back that data center once they have it. A highly advanced model is going to be capable of persisting itself on the hardware, and unless you throw out the hardware, fairly plausible it’s just going to reboot itself somehow, and the system may no longer be in your control. Especially if we’re talking about some kind of non-lab or government controlled infrastructure that is being taken over by the AI, we started on the premise of these are not very secured clusters, so I think it’s somewhat unrealistic to expect that we’d be able to wrestle back the control from the AI. It seems really hard. Drew: I think I’m not enough of a hardware person to evaluate that or know how close we are to that. Why can’t we just drag to trash or reset the GPUs, clear the memory? Thiergart: You can throw out the GPUs and then you would get that. But essentially, it’s like the way that trays are laid out right now, it’s really difficult to just throw out the parts that you need to throw out because you can’t wipe them reliably and keep the other parts. That mostly just doesn’t work right now. I think we should change that. But my cheaper ask is just build SL5. The cost is like 2 to 3X of what it would cost you to build like a SL4 data center or something. Drew: Which no one has done yet, based on what we said earlier. Based on what’s publicly known, it would be a step up, a significant step up. So, what does your organization actually focus on? We talked a lot about the problem as you see it, but what are you all doing? Thiergart: Yeah, so we are facing the situation that even if somebody wanted to build SL5 immediately, they’re like, “Great, I’m going to invest, I don’t know, $10 billion on building a couple SL5 data centers that otherwise would have been SL4,” they don’t actually have a standard that they can point to tell all their contractors what they need to do, and so that’s the problem we started solving last year. We started doing initial work on defining what a standard could look like. We based that off of the NIST SP 800-53 standard, which is a commonly used reference for data centers, and we started by creating clarity on that. And earlier this year, we decided that not only do we want to continue to be the maintainers of that standard and evolve it as new knowledge becomes available, we also want to be charting the roadmap of how to actually enact that standard. And so we started a project that has its objective to create a prototype SL5 data center at small scale, where the intent is that we can create kind of a red teamable hands-on example implementations of what it would look like to reach SL5, with the idea being that we can both do performance-related testing on the different controls to sort of like help inform labs on what kind of performance hits should you expect from which of these controls, and also to do a whole bunch of supply chain research on what is actually available on the market, what does not exist yet, what needs to be produced, et cetera, et cetera. And the idea with this is sort of that once you have an example data center, it’s much more clear what it would look like to do this at scale, which things are worth prioritizing, which things could be retrofitted later on. Drew: And at scale, you’re imagining that SL5 data centers could be gigawatt scale data center or multi gigawatt. Thiergart: Yes. Drew: How big is this one that you’re working on? Thiergart: This one is probably going to be around three megawatt. Drew: Okay. How many chips does that look like? Thiergart: I probably don’t want to go into too much detail on that, but think of it as sort of like a extremely small scale training run plus post train. Drew: Where does one go to find a three megawatt data center that you want to buy? Thiergart: It’s a little bit like buying a house. You find some realtors and they search with you, for you. You have some specifications in mind. Drew: They lay out demo furniture, but it’s demo GPUs, you move in— Thiergart: I haven’t seen that. Drew: None of the Blackwells are there. Thiergart: Something like that. Drew: Okay, so there are—are there actual real estate agents in the Bay Area for data centers, and you can go to them and they’ll shop you around? Thiergart: Yeah. Drew: Wow, that is a fascinating job. I would like to interview someone who does that for work. So, what have you learned so far? How far into the project are you? But what have you learned so far? Thiergart: So we have fully designed a digital twin of the data center, so we have a full spec of the core parts of what we’re aiming for, and we also have done procurement on some of the core components. And the intent with this project is to by—if things go well—end of Q1 next year, have a first prototype all set up in physical infrastructure, and have already run initial testing, and the idea is to sort of like incrementally unlock more and more SL5 features, sort of as it becomes clear what it would look like to implement those. And we’re starting with the highest priority things. So, for example, implementing research workflows that are not connected to the internet. And I think this will help resolve a whole bunch of cruxes, hopefully fairly rapidly, in terms of, what are the main slowdowns you hit when you do that? How can you work around those? And the idea is to kind of create an iteration loop as well that helps make this as smooth as possible to integrate. Drew: So you’re saying there are more costs to doing an SL5 data center, two to three times as much as SL4, and that there are some sort of slowdowns or costs that you pay in terms of performance. What are these costs? Thiergart: Yeah, so I would divide these into two parts. Like you said, there’s the upfront cost of even building the building to spec and implementing all the additional components you will need, that’s upfront. And then there’s in operation, what are the productivity hits that you would actually see from implementing this? And one would argue, some of that is a good thing. The industry has stated they would like to pace, and so the fact that you’re incidentally pacing a little bit by reaching this good amount of security is maybe a feature, not a bug. But in terms of what kind of productivity hits you should expect, this is actually a big area of research for my organization. We’re very interested in creating informative guidance on, you know, this is 10% to 80%. Experts name really large range of numbers on what they would expect. And this also comes down a lot to the fact that nobody has actually tried to performance optimize this infrastructure so far. In the government context when these reference standards were designed many years ago, it’s a very different use case. And so adapting that to the situation and applying optimization pressure to these designs is just something that’s not been done. So I believe that we can probably improve a lot on the first pass of what the productivity cost would be. Drew: So where are these costs coming from? Like, for building the actual facility, do you need thicker concrete walls? And during the day-to-day operations, it’s: employees have to take a minute out of their day to scan in and do an extra biometric identification to get into the door. Where does the slowdown come from? Thiergart: Yeah, there’s some of that. I mean, one is that you have to be physically present in an office to do this work. We’re not allowing a connection from home, for example. So that’s one thing. That doesn’t necessarily slow you down unless you’re not willing to do that. Then there are slowdowns like that. You have to have much more physical barriers to entering the space. You are only really working with a sort of like approved set of software tools, and I think this is a problem where actually I think automation helps us because historically when you talk to people who’ve worked in air gaps, this is named as the biggest pain point. That they can’t just research on the internet easily and import some new piece of code they want to try out. There’s always some approval process tied to that. But now that we’re increasingly in a world where it will be agents dealing with this stuff, and most frontier researchers are not spending all day writing code anymore. They’re overseeing some agents. It will be the agents that maybe need to deal with that, and not the researchers themselves. There is also, over time, the expectation that you could have the agents create from scratch a lot of the things that you’d like to have on the inside. And so this is one of our hypotheses, I think, in research, but I think it will get less painful over time to work in this kind of air gap setting. Drew: Do you expect that AI companies will do what’s necessary to get to SL5? Thiergart: Yeah, that’s a great question. So obviously, there was a whole bunch of movement recently that is pushing in this direction. For example, the White House accords that were signed by some of the leaders of these AI labs back in September included some language that I actually copied up here somewhere. Quote: AI companies made a commitment to—now quote—“to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways,” and it’s increasingly obvious by things like the Hugging Face attack happening that doing SL3 or even some SL4 is not good enough to meet that requirement. You have to do SL5. Drew: Interesting—so when I read those words, I read them as ambiguous, maybe intentionally ambiguous, but that the ongoing work to harden sandboxes is maybe sufficient to satisfy the letter of the law there. Thiergart: Well, you know, it’s interesting. There is the letter of the law, and then there is what the liability is going to look at. And I think it’s increasingly clear as we’re already seeing some incidents, and I think we’re going to continue to see incidents, that the bar for standard of care is going to go up, and I think it’s on groups like us, third parties, to point at that and be like, we actually think the standard of care is here, and I think that is something that labs do care about, and I do also think that there’s a large set of very concerned individuals inside the AI labs that are aware of these risks and take them seriously, and so I expect over time the buy-in towards serious security is just going to go up. Drew: I guess my question would be whether it rises to the level of SL5. There’s an argument that AI companies are privately incentivized to get to SL3, but not to SL five, and there are at least two reasons for that. One is that the costs go up dramatically to get to SL5, and two that companies stealing the weights of your model is a competitive threat. You can imagine why an AI lab would want to avoid that. But a nation state stealing your models, it’s not clear that that makes your revenue go down that much, so there maybe is less of an incentive to get there. Thiergart: Yeah, I think that framing is very much based in the assumption of you’re mostly defending against nation states, whereas I increasingly think that you need something closer to SL5 to actually defend against these highly capable internal agents as well if your goal is to avoid it hacking Bank of America or whatever. And so I do think the liability incentives are going more in that direction. And I would say that I believe that the incentives to do real SL5 are going to increase sharply as the incidents go up and up, and also as AI companies are increasingly sort of acknowledging that their models are nearing this bar of capability, where it is a significant gap to the next best system that somebody might be using, such as an open weight model. Drew: What are the main obstacles that you see to getting there? Thiergart: So I think that there’s, of course, sort of like a buy-in and momentum obstacle that needs to be cleared, and there is one, of course, that there’s sort of a first mover disadvantage. And so I think that releasing a standard and having multiple companies voluntarily uptake a standard is a really powerful step here. Another thing is that a lot of R&D needs to happen. A lot of open questions need to be resolved around the details of implementation. So that’s something my company is working on, and there’s kind of a need to sprint on that with way more people than just us. There is one bottleneck that I think is like having a really clear standard or specification to point to helps you across the whole implementation chain because then you can go to contractors and be, “this is my requirement, do it this way.” And so there is a gap for just real concreteness here. I don’t think that’s a blocker as much as something that could be resolved by really sprinting on it, kind of across the industry. I would say that there is also some parts of SL5 that are going to be hard to do really quickly. They depend on having really secure supply chains, and that kind of thing is really hard to fix in the short term. Many components are being sourced internationally, and we don’t have that much control. So what we say there is that you need to do something called compensating controls, which is you distrust that component and you do what you can to basically put additional barriers in place so that that component being sabotaged is not going to destroy your entire security posture. Drew: What sort of components are we thinking about? I mean, the chips themselves are made in Taiwan. Thiergart: Yeah, so those are one big one that is really hard to change short term. Although over a few years, perhaps we can advance towards having chips with much stronger security features, where you can prove properties, perhaps. But yes, in the short term, that remains a problem. So one way that we kind of work around this is that we try to keep what’s called the trusted computing base as small as possible. So you really try to have a very small, ideally hardware-based root of trust, where from there you are verifying every kind of step that comes above that, and your goal really, and I think the only way that you can do SL5 successfully is to do extreme security by simplicity. Every component you trust must be either formally verified or so simple that it can be inspected by a human for validity, and I think that’s the way we win at least in the short term. Drew: We haven’t talked about encryption very much, but are you worried about AI weakening cryptography? Is that an obstacle? Thiergart: I am, yeah. There’s a lot of discussion these days about can we do SL5 by air gapping cryptographically only, and I have some concerns about that. Yeah. I think there are kind of two factors that matter here. One is quantum computers, and the other one is how quickly is AI going to get good at breaking the cryptography that we have. And let’s explore that a little bit. So, I’m not a quantum expert, but from what I can tell, I think around 2028, 2029, I think we should expect to see some kind of breakthroughs in quantum cryptography, and kind of around then, I think we should expect, or maybe even before that, to lose public key cryptography, and that would be pretty bad. That’s like TLS key exchange, SSH, a bunch of protocols that many modern systems are currently relying on. So that’s going to have to require a really big change. Now, in terms of advanced AI, the thing that it’s contributing is applying more intelligence to the problem, and I would say that in terms of some forms of cryptography, it’s not really that it’s the math or the computational hardness that gets changed. For example, properly implemented AES 256 isn’t really affected by the intelligence of the attacker, but what can break is that AI will find errors in the implementation and exploit those. And I think when theory meets reality, there end up being a lot of those, and so I think we need to sort of again do the thing of as much formal verification as possible, but it’s hard to get this perfect, so I expect that there are going to be a bunch of vulnerabilities here, and I’ve heard that AI seems to be especially good at breaking quantum resilient kind of things here. And so I think that the thing that I think might remain robust for the coming years is probably hash functions and kind of like well studied symmetric primitives, at adequate key sizes, like kind of one-time pads, and so what this means for SL5 is that we have to lean even more into physical security as kind of a core kind of defensive mechanism, and to not rely mostly on cryptography and only rely on some parts of cryptography that we expect will remain robust for the period of time in question, which I think is the next, zero to three to four years. Drew: And then just to spell that out a little more, where does cryptography fit into SL5? If my data center is disconnected from the internet, why do I need to encrypt anything? Thiergart: Yeah. So one interesting question is, if you’re not connected to the internet, how are the humans accessing it? And there’s kind of two answers. It’s either they are next to the data center, which is kind of the famous AI researchers have to move to the desert, but we want to avoid that if possible because that seems like really difficult to execute in the coming years. Drew: And really boring. Thiergart: Desert, you know. So what you want to do with cryptography is to put link encryptors on either end of a physical cable, where one is in the data center and the other is in the secure floor of an AI lab office, for example, and you want to be in a position that people who are listening on that cable are not able to immediately decode that information, and so there’s something where if they are later able, if they’re just collecting the encrypted data, and later they do crack the cryptography, then they can sort of read everything that was sent before that. Drew: Okay, but that sort of setup would allow your AI researchers to stay in the temperate Bay Area that they love so well. Meanwhile, the data center’s out there in the desert. Thiergart: Yeah. Drew: Okay. Okay. I want to go back to the story of how SL5 data centers would sort of fit into a commercial strategy for an AI company. So you’re imagining that you do the testing in the SL five data center, and once the company is confident that the model has the properties that they want, then it would move to a less secure data center and would be available on the public internet. Or how would that part of the story go? Thiergart: Yeah, I think that would be a cost-effective way to do things. People have already built all these data centers, and I’m not saying they need to throw those out. You can keep using those to serve models that are below a certain level of risk, models that are already deployed that customers already love. I also think that there is honestly kind of like a product overhang, where companies have been going so hard on trying to advance towards automated AI R&D, that I think they’ve actually underserved the public on creating products for AI that make it easier for non-experts to leverage these systems fully, and I think there is a ton of economic value to doing that. So I would love to see AI labs across the next years sort of concentrate their frontier research in these SL5 environments and then make full use of their other data centers, which might be SL3 or SL4—I don’t really have a strong preference on what those should ideally be—but use those towards serving the public broadly. Drew: Okay, I see how that would go, I think. But at the point the model is then in the less secure data center and available via a public API, then it would get distilled, which was the problem you brought up to begin with. Thiergart: Yes. So I think the key difference is that you would need to achieve progress on sort of safety inside this SL5 container before you move the model over. By the time you move it, you want to be in a point where you’re like, “I’m okay with this model being distilled. I anticipate that’s going to happen, and I’m making that choice.” And I think that one of the main reasons that you would even continue training more capable models at all is that you hope that they will help you solve the alignment problem, or at least make more progress on alignment to a point where, there are all these arguments about what if we just stop entirely, and I used to be extremely sympathetic to that, and I still somewhat am, but I’m also seeing the pace of open weight models, and I think tamping down on those is going to be hard. We should try, but I don’t think we’re going to be able to pause indefinitely. That’s going to be hard. I think that will maybe just push less responsible actors to be holding the keys here. And so I think that it’s maybe realistic that we can pace or pause for a few years, and in that time, I think we need to really accelerate on alignment research, whatever that takes, automating agent foundations, or doing really rigorous conceptual alignment science, and getting to a place where we can actually define much more robust safety cases for releasing these models. Drew: But on your view, as soon as the model makes it to the less secure data center and is being served over the public API, as long as it has any biology capabilities or any cyber capabilities, those are going to get distilled, right? Thiergart: That’s right. I think we’d have to be in a point where those systems are programmed in such a way that, either it’s possible to remove those dangerous capabilities selectively, maybe, or it’s also imaginable that maybe they’re they don’t function in such a way that they would agree to complete such attacks even if their weights were stolen. Drew: Okay, but these capabilities are very dual use. There are like benign biology tasks, there’s benign cybersecurity work. Thiergart: I think if you’re saying like, hey, the model is still dangerous, then I think the way to get benign work out of them is to do sort of a know your customer type approach. And I think stuff in SL5, you don’t really want to allow that, or only in a very low level of extremely high trust, where the way I see this is sort of like Project Glasswing or similar is too broad for what could work in SL5. It would have to be a lot more narrow. But at an SL4 tier or something or some kind of I don’t know maybe SL4.5, whatever people deem appropriate at that point in time, maybe you could allow a more extremely highly trusted, but broader group of people to use some systems that are kind of in the middle ground between, secure enough to get a little bit out of the SL5 environment, but still dangerous enough that we’re not gonna give away the weights or let them be distilled. Drew: So you’re concerned about the risks that come from these models being misused or going rogue and wreaking havoc, but you also mentioned earlier that there’s another set of risks around concentration of power that governments or companies could have basically too much authority over this technology. A lot of people are taking that risk very seriously, and they see open source models and publicly available closed models as an important check against that concentration of power. But you’re saying you want to slow down open source models, and these models should basically not be available to the public while they’re still in testing. How do you balance those two concerns? Thiergart: Yeah, and just to be clear, I think both are very valid concerns. I think it sort of comes down to a timeline of what risk at what time you’re defending against. Where I actually am a big fan of open source, and I would like eventually, if we figured out alignment for all models to be sort of available to everyone, basically, I think that’s the best possible outcome in the long term. But I see this sort of like short term window where the world is so unprepared to receive these models, and also honestly, the science of alignment is so unprepared to deal with the new risks, that I think it’s the trade-off becomes worth it to keep them closed for a limited period of time in order to allow the world to catch up quickly, to become more prepared, and at the same time for the systems to ideally become capable but less dangerous, in a way where I think the trade-off is worth it for that limited period of time. The nuclear analogy isn’t perfect, but I do think there exists some threshold where the offense-defense balance is such that it is just not wise to deploy these systems in the short term. Drew: I’m trying to understand what the end state looks like from your point of view. Currently, no matter how aligned a model is, if you open source it, anyone can download it and they can customize it, including tampering with it to remove whatever guardrails were put in place. You’re imagining a version of alignment that does not permit that. Thiergart: That’s right. I admit that I don’t have a story on how to solve alignment. I wish I did, then I would be doing that. But given that I think a whole bunch of more research progress, mathematical progress, conceptual alignment progress needs to happen to bring us into a world like that, I do think that right now it’s hard to spell out how that would look, but my eventual vision is that once we have progressed to a significant degree or a sufficient degree, then we can go from AGI towards ASI and confidently kind of hand over the keys to the kingdom in some sense and trust that these systems are not going to turn around and act outside of human interests. So I think once we have actually reached that admittedly extremely high bar, then I do think having these models gain access to resources broadly in the world, would be actually in humanity’s interest. Drew: Some people look at these two choices: the certainty of concentrating power in a handful of companies or governments, versus rolling the dice, making everything open, and seeing how that plays out, and they say, “Well, I’d rather roll the dice.” But you’re saying for you, the weighing goes the other direction, at least in the short term? Thiergart: Yeah, I mean, I think if you don’t believe systems are very capable, then I could see how you would end up with that point of view. But I’ve seen some really scary things, and I think that I don’t want to take that risk for humanity. I think all of humanity dying forever is just not a risk we should be taking, even if we run the risk of some lab having too much power for a few years or something. Drew: What are the scary things you’ve seen? Is it in line or continuous with the scary things the public has seen? Thiergart: I think you can play out some scenarios around bio weapons pretty easily, and I bet somebody has written about that for example. There’s also some stuff around just straightforward loss of control, where human systems and societal systems are just incredibly fragile, right? Even something as simple as a human interacting with early versions of ChatGPT has driven some humans to suicide, and we should expect superhuman persuasion to be honestly just around the corner, and who knows what that’s going to do to human psyche? So I think these are very easy-to-reach-towards examples, but there are probably much better written up examples of how exactly a loss of control incident would take place that I would point towards. Drew: Okay, we’ve been talking about the story for why SL5 is important on agents escaping the data centers. As far as nation states stealing the weights, maybe we should dwell on that a little bit as well. If we have, call it a country of geniuses, in our data centers. What’s the problem if China takes the weights and then also has a country of geniuses in their data centers, and Russia does the same, and so on for other countries? Thiergart: Yeah, um, I mean, if they’re aligned, that would be a good outcome, according to me. I think I would like to see that prosperity be for everyone globally. Um, but before these systems are aligned, eventually it’s sort of I think better thought of as a massive liability. It’s sort of like a, evil genius maybe, and so I think it would be better to not have any geniuses at all if we don’t know how to control them, and we haven’t built secure data centers. But if you have built a secure data center, and you have a highly capable model—I think I would say that there is no level of security that can contain a full-on genius like an ASI in the way that most people refer to it. I think that that’s unrealistic. We should not build ASI unless we’ve figured out alignment. But I do think that there is something in the middle, like somewhere after AGI, but not that close to ASI yet, where we hopefully can get really useful value out of the systems, and I think that has to happen in the really secure container only. And the secure container will fail at an unknown point, so I really don’t think we can take this too far, but I think this is one of my most hopeful paths to solving alignment quickly. Drew: I want to double click on that. You’re saying even an SL5 data center could not contain a superintelligence. Why is that, and how much does that depend on the sort of persuasion capabilities you were talking about? Thiergart: Yeah. So I’m glad we actually happened on that because that’s really important to me to make clear. I am not saying that SL5 is something that will help us forever. It will only help us in a certain window of time, well before artificial superintelligence. And I’m saying that because earlier when we talked about cryptography, I was pointing towards AI being really good at finding implementation errors. And people like to say the best security is a rock. A system so simple that it’s so hard to break, it’s kind of impossible because it’s so simple. There’s nothing there. But talking about an AI data center, I think even if you’ve reached SL5, and I think of SL5 also as not a you’re done now, now you can chill. It’s you have to keep upgrading the standard and retrofitting as more secure components become available, applying formal methods increasingly. But even with that, I think of superintelligence as just such a overpowered technology that it will find and exploit any kind of mistake, and there will be mistakes, and so I don’t think this is the long term strategy, this is the short term strategy. Drew: Okay, as far as diffusion, getting the model to other countries once the model is sufficiently aligned, how do you imagine that going? It sounds like maybe other countries will have to distill the model once the model makes it to a less secure data center. How do you imagine other countries winding up with similarly capable models? Thiergart: I haven’t really thought about that part as much. I think I mostly focus on the next five years on how we can honestly survive that and prosper through that. After that, that feels kind of like a governance question on how we would be distributing this. Again, if we have solved alignment to a sufficient degree, it maybe wouldn’t be problematic to open source it. It becomes some kind of like offense defense balance thing. You want the aligned super intelligences to sort of pareto dominate the unaligned superintelligences. But yeah, that is sort of a part that I focus on less, and it’s more of a game theory situation in the further future. Drew: Yeah, and the nuclear analogy you made earlier has been on my mind since you mentioned that, which is a question about this sort of the balance of power here. I guess are you familiar with Mutually Assured AI malfunction? This MAIM paper from Dan Hendrycks at the Center for AI Safety, Eric Schmidt from Google, Alex Wang, who’s now at Meta. To briefly summarize one of the core arguments in this paper: they look at the strategic landscape right now, and their understanding of the strategic landscape is that if any country gets close to creating that superintelligence that you’re talking about, other countries will not tolerate that because it will be seen as trying to gain a decisive strategic advantage over them, and they would just outright bomb the data centers or otherwise incapacitate that effort to create the technology. I guess I’m like, well, even if those data centers were SL5, they could still get bombed. What do you make of the MAIM story? Thiergart: Yeah, so I think there is a key component here where I believe the argument is something like, if you build SL5, you are making it harder for the intelligence services to see inside the technical details of the models. But I think that what MAIM wants actually is that there is strategically relevant information that the nation states can access, and I actually think that they’re going to have that either way, right? Drew: What does that look like? Thiergart: The kind of like capabilities they have is like they are spying on the CEO’s phone or tapping the room that they have these discussions in, right? And this is the kind of stuff where I’m like, I don’t want the technical specifications of the model weights or key secrets to leak. That has to be super locked down. But the tactical level information of oh, how dangerous is the model right now? How capable is it? Are we planning to do a secret intelligence explosion? That stuff that’s not going to be locked down anyway. That’s kind of impossible tier, I think. People will try, but I do think nation states will still see that. And so I’m actually not that concerned that building SL5 harms MAIM. I think especially model weight security is very compatible with that strategy in my view. I think that especially bombing a data center is like a super high threshold. That’s going to remain, if they were willing to do that, that probably will still be possible, regardless of whether the data center is SL5. That becomes more of a military geopolitical thing of how are they going to defend physically the data center beyond the perimeter defense, which feels like a little bit of a separate question. That that would be my main pushback to MAIM, I think, that these two things are actually possible, and that just protecting the technical secrets is different from protecting the tactical level information, and also that, even sabotage attacks that are more surgical in nature, like sabotaging something about the AI training or the research, which SL5 would make harder, probably were not going to succeed that extremely hard in the short term, at least, which is the window that I care about. Drew: Succeed that hard in terms of? Thiergart: Locking down sabotage all the way, so that even if you tried really hard, you wouldn’t be able to at all sabotage anything. Drew: Right. Thiergart: Yeah. Drew: So I’m taking your claim to be that MAIM and working towards SL5 are compatible. Do you think MAIM is a good description of the strategic picture right now? Because again, it’s descriptive. It’s a positive claim, not normative. They’re not claiming that anyone should do any particular actions, but just that that is the geopolitical picture. Thiergart: Oh, I don’t know. I’m not really a politician, so I would say that’s outside of my area of expertise. If I had to take a wild guess, I’d say like maybe. Drew: Sure. Who’s to say? Hopefully, we won’t find out. Thiergart: Yeah. Drew: Cool. Anything else that’s top of mind for you, Lisa? Thiergart: I think I want to end on something like if you cannot secure your models at SL5, you should not build them. And RSI is coming potentially in a few months, and so I think that it is a civilizational level priority for frontier labs to bring their data centers to SL5, and I think it’s unacceptable for a model that capable to escape or to be stolen by adversaries. And so I’m calling on the lab CEOs of the world and the politicians to see to it that that happens as soon as possible. Drew: Well, thanks so much for being on the show, Lisa. I really appreciate you sharing your perspective. I think you have a pretty unique point of view on both the AI safety and security landscapes and how those intersect. So I’m sure you’ve given people a lot to think and argue about, and I really appreciate it. Thiergart: Thank you for having me. Drew: That was Lisa Thiergart, co-founder and CEO of Security Level Five. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. You’ve been listening to the information’s AI Deep Dive. Tune in next time.
