title: Perovskite Connect 2026 in review: 30% growth, top keynotes and what our attendees said
content:
Perovskite Connect 2026 in review: 30% growth, top keynotes and what our attendees said
Last month we held
Perovskite Connect 2026
at the Estrel Convention Center in Berlin, co-located with TechBlick's Future of Electronics RESHAPED. It was only the second edition of the event, and attendance grew by about 30% over last year. Since then we have asked attendees, speakers and exhibitors what they thought, and the feedback was great. Here is a short look back, and a look ahead to 2027.
A full room for the opening keynotes at Perovskite Connect 2026
The keynotes
The conference opened with keynotes from Oxford PV, CubicPV, GCL and Microquanta, and the second day opened with Qcells, Caelux, Tandem PV and SolarEdge. Together, these talks gave a clear picture of where perovskite tandems stand on their way to the market:
Oxford PV
spoke about the era of perovskite-on-silicon, and what it takes to bring tandem solar modules to market.
discussed how accelerated testing and energy yield analysis can establish the bankability of perovskite products.
Microquanta
both presented their four-terminal tandem strategies, an approach that avoids the current-matching constraints of two-terminal devices.
described scaling perovskite-silicon tandems from lab records to production on industrial M10 wafers, and
shared the wins and the remaining challenges of producing and deploying 1x2 meter perovskite products.
Tandem PV
talked about its path to bankability for perovskite/silicon tandem panels, and
SolarEdge
showed how module-level power electronics can protect the gains of tandem modules from mismatch losses.
The exhibition area at the Estrel
Beyond the keynotes, the program had many more strong talks. Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin presented its Solar TAP approach to turning perovskite innovation into impact, imec/EnergyVille covered structures and processes for upscaling perovskite modules and tandems, and ZSW presented a recycling procedure for perovskite minimodules. The day before the conference was dedicated to masterclasses and tours, including a tour of HZB.
The main topics
The talks covered the whole perovskite value chain, and a few themes came up again and again:
Tandems move to the fab
: perovskite-silicon tandems were the clear focus, with both two-terminal and four-terminal approaches on show, and many talks on the path from lab cells to full-size wafers and modules.
Bankability and reliability
: accelerated stress testing, energy yield, encapsulation and LED-based stability testing, with talks from CubicPV, Tandem PV, Eternal Sun, Everlight and H.B. Fuller.
Production tools and processes
: roll-to-roll production (Energy Materials Corporation, nextCoatema, ROWO Coating), inkjet printing (UniJet, Dracula Technologies), spatial ALD (Kalpana), laser processing (Bergfeld Lasertech) and contactless metallization (HighLine Technology).
Materials and inks
: metal oxide transport layers (Sofab Inks, TU Dortmund), interface materials (Nano-C), printable ITO inks (PINA Creation), organic transport materials (LinXole) and the high-purity materials needed for reproducible manufacturing (Noctiluca).
New module designs and sustainability
: Power Roll's ITO-free micro-groove modules, Homerun Energy's vertically integrated value chain, and ZSW's work on recycling.
Overall, the message from Berlin was that perovskites are moving from lab records to production lines, and that the focus now is on bankability, reliability and cost at scale.
What attendees said
We received a lot of great feedback. Here are some of our favorites:
"The event was truly excellent, striking the perfect balance between scientific and technological insights and industrial perspectives. The presentations provided a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art and the progress being made towards the industrialization of various technologies. The exhibition area was also a great opportunity to connect and exchange ideas with leading companies in the field."
- Luigi Vesce, University of Rome Tor Vergata
"I found the Perovskite Connect event to be excellent. The agenda was very relevant and everyone stayed on time and on topic. Having several of the leaders in this industry (Oxford, GCL, Tandem, Cubic, etc) made the networking extremely valuable."
- David McDougall, H.B. Fuller
"I thought the event was very well organised, with a really high quality of companies attending and some excellent presentations. The overall energy and networking were very good too."
- Neil Spann, Power Roll
"Thank you for a fantastic event. It was extremely useful for us as an early-stage start-up. The masterclass and talks were high quality and very practical, the HZB tour was a highlight, and the networking drinks led to several valuable new connections."
- Nathaniel Davis, TwoPhold
"The event was very well organized and a lot of interesting contributions were given."
- Immo Koetschau, Oxford PV
If you attended and missed a talk, all the presentations were recorded and are available to attendees on TechBlick's event platform.
Join us in 2027: speak, exhibit, sponsor
We're already working on
Perovskite Connect 2027
, which will be held on October 20-21, 2027 at the Estrel Convention Center in Berlin, with masterclasses and tours on October 19. Perovskite Connect will again be co-located with TechBlick's Future of Electronics RESHAPED, a major gathering for the printed, flexible and roll-to-roll electronics industries.
We expect the event to keep growing. Tandem production lines are coming online, and more perovskite companies are moving from pilot lines to products. If your company works on perovskite materials, equipment, cells, modules or testing, this is the place to show your work to the people who matter.
If you would like to present, exhibit or sponsor in 2027, please
contact us now
. Early conversations get the best speaking slots, booth locations and sponsorship options. You can also
register to attend here
. See you in Berlin!

title: Perovskite nanocrystal LEDs reach four times higher efficiency without a ligand-exchange step
content:
Perovskite nanocrystal LEDs reach four times higher efficiency without a ligand-exchange step
Researchers at Kookmin University, Sungkyunkwan University and Hanyang University have developed perovskite nanocrystal LEDs that need no separate post-synthetic ligand-exchange process, reaching a maximum external quantum efficiency of 11.4%, around four times the 2.7% obtained from conventionally synthesized nanocrystals.
Perovskite nanocrystals are attractive for display LEDs for their high luminescence efficiency, color purity and solution processability, but nanocrystals from conventional synthesis come coated in large quantities of organic ligands with long hydrocarbon chains. Those chains impede charge transport between neighboring nanocrystals, so building a high-performance device has generally required a post-synthetic step to swap the long-chain ligands for shorter ones. Much recent work has approached the problem through ligand design instead, including
an “all-in-one” organic ligand for emissive nanocrystals
a strategy that reached 31.7% EQE
Rather than treating the surfaces after synthesis, the team controlled the nanocrystals’ surface chemistry from the synthesis stage, using a heat-up method based on a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction. The resulting films showed lower energetic disorder and more ordered crystalline structures than films made from conventionally synthesized nanocrystals, along with significantly improved charge transport between nanocrystals. These nanocrystals were then incorporated directly into the emissive layer of the devices.

title: i-Components says a customer will test its perovskite barrier film in space this year
content:
i-Components says a customer will test its perovskite barrier film in space this year
Korea-based barrier film maker
i-Components
says it has supplied samples of a space-grade barrier film for perovskite solar cells to global space companies. The company says one customer plans to test a flexible perovskite solar cell in space within the year.
Barrier films protect perovskite cells from moisture and oxygen, and the company says durability is critical for space-grade cells that must keep their performance in extreme conditions. i-Components says it is working with perovskite solar cell makers in Japan and China to validate film quality and improve its specifications, and that it has the quality and mass-production capability to supply products to customer requirements.
The company says it has invested a total of 25.5 billion won (about US$19 million) to add production lines for barrier films for displays and solar cells, and plans to expand beyond displays into solar. “We will prepare for development and mass production of barrier films in step with the commercialization pace of perovskite solar cells, from ground applications to space,” a company official said.

title: 机制搭台 场景拓展——浙江省整县光伏试点（钱塘区）建设经验-索比光伏网
content:
浙江省发展改革委深入贯彻党中央、国务院关于碳达峰碳中和的决策部署，落实国家能源局整县屋顶
开发试点部署，制定《浙江省光伏发电高质量发展三年行动方案(2026—2028年)》，将杭州市钱塘区等11个县(市、区)列为整县示范，加强调度指导，推动试点地区先行探索、形成经验。在浙江省发展改革委指导下，杭州市钱塘区把整县光伏试点建设作为全域低碳建设的重要抓手，坚持机制搭台、资源挖潜、场景拓展、效益转化一体推进，试点建设取得阶段性成效。目前，该地光伏装机已达200万千瓦，成为浙江省首个集中式光伏装机超百万千瓦的区县，有力支撑区内2个省级零碳园区创建。
一、强化“三端协同”，夯实试点落地支撑
一是高位统筹建机制。钱塘区将整县光伏试点作为区委、区政府重点工作，成立由主要负责同志任双组长的工作专班，系统构建“134X”工作体系，即锚定三年新增装机不低于200万千瓦、总量翻番的总目标，聚焦工业、地面、机构3个特色领域，打造园区、建筑、交通、农旅4个“光伏+”融合应用场景，因地制宜培育X个创新示范场景。二是全域排摸绘底图。地毯式摸排光伏资源，形成255万平方米工业园区屋顶、15万平方米公共机构屋顶、1.5万余亩坑塘水面3张资源清单，绘制全域开发“一张图”，全部建成后光伏装机可突破350万千瓦。三是流程重塑提效率。建立新型光伏项目备案管理机制，出台区级
项目开发建设管理办法，探索容缺办理机制，推动项目从立项到并网审批周期压缩60%以上。
二、强化“四维发力”，拓展光伏应用场景
一是推动“光伏+园区”全面铺开。综合采用“自投自建”“屋顶租赁”等开发模式，推动存量工业园区屋顶“能建尽建”，到2028年形成碳排替代空间17万吨。二是推广“光伏+建筑”一体集成。大力推广BIPV光伏建筑一体化应用，加快推进党政机关、高校等公共机构15万平方米屋顶空间光伏建设。三是打造“光伏+交通”共建共享。统筹利用园区道路、交通主干道和农田机耕路等闲置资源，推动辖区内高速收费站、港区光伏建设全覆盖，实现清洁能源100%消纳。四是深化“光伏+农旅”一地两用。迭代升级“渔光互补”复合开发模式，形成全省首个超百万千瓦级“渔光互补”集群，年发电量预计超12亿度。
三、强化“三链联动”，放大试点综合效益
一是做优惠企链。坚持“以光伏降成本、以绿电增效益”，推动工商业光伏“应上尽上”，降低企业用能成本，同步探索绿电直连。以全省首个绿电直连项目为例，项目实现绿电精准溯源和产品碳足迹核算，投运后每年可减少碳关税支出近千万元。二是做实富民链。坚持发展成果全民共享，推广“企业投资+村集体出租”发展模式，让农户屋顶、机耕路等闲置资源变成可持续的增收资产。临江街道东庄村利用7万平方米闲置空间打造的光伏项目年内投用，预计每年为村集体增收50万元。三是做强产业链。把丰沛绿电资源作为牵引产业转型、强链补链的重要抓手，今年以来已招引落地绿色能源产业项目7个、总投资近百亿元。目前全区共集聚绿色能源产业规上企业79家，其中国家级绿色工厂14家。
下一步，省发展改革委将围绕碳达峰碳中和目标，持续强化全省整县光伏试点统筹，进一步加强规划衔接、政策指导和跟踪调度，及时总结提炼试点地区在机制搭台、场景拓展、绿电直连等方面的经验做法，通过政策解读、案例推广等方式推动在全省复制应用，为全省新型能源体系建设提供有力支撑。

title: 广期所：调整多晶硅期货相关合约交易手续费标准-索比光伏网
content:
广期所11月11日发布公告，调整多晶硅、碳酸锂期货相关合约交易手续费标准。
关于多晶硅期货PS2711合约、碳酸锂期LC2711合约有关事项的公告
经研究决定，现将多晶硅期货PS2711、碳酸锂期货LC2711合约有关事项公告如下：
多晶硅期货PS2711合约交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之一、日内平今仓交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之二点五，交易指令每次最小下单数量中的每次最小开仓下单数量为5手、每次最小平仓下单数量为1手，非期货公司会员或者客户单日开仓量不得超过200手。
碳酸锂期货LC2711合约交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之零点八、日内平今仓交易手续费标准为成交金额的万分之零点八，交易指令每次最小下单数量中的每次最小开仓下单数量为2手、每次最小平仓下单数量为1手，非期货公司会员或者客户单日开仓量不得超过800手。
单日开仓量是指非期货公司会员或者客户当日在单个合约上的买开仓数量与卖开仓数量之和。套期保值交易、做市交易的单日开仓数量不受上述标准限制。具有实际控制关系的账户按照一个账户管理。

title: 全国首个省级电力市场 纠纷调解机构成立！-索比光伏网
content:
为进一步健全陕西省电力市场矛盾纠纷多元化解机制，妥善处置电力市场化交易中的各类争议，依法保护各类经营主体合法权益，维护公平有序的电力市场秩序，近日，陕西省发改委、西北能源监管局联合印发通知，组建陕西省电力市场纠纷调解委员会（以下简称“调委会”）。
调委会将聚焦纠纷受理与调解处置、调解员队伍建设、制度规则建设、纠纷研判与风险预警、政策宣贯与咨询服务、协同联动与闭环管理等方面履行职责，受理发电企业、售电公司、电力用户、电力交易机构、电力调度机构以及虚拟电厂、独立储能、分布式电源聚合商等新型经营主体在电力中长期交易、现货交易、合同履约、电量计量与结算、电价执行、绿电绿证交易、辅助服务与需求侧响应等业务中产生的民事商事争议。
下一步，西北能源监管局将与陕西省发改委一道，加强业务指导和监督，推动调委会公平公正开展调解，促进电力市场矛盾源头化解、就地化解，为全省电力市场健康有序发展提供有力保障。

title: EGL3 secures marine infrastructure licence for Scottish waters
content:
A marine infrastructure licence has been granted for Eastern Green Link
3 (EGL3), a joint venture between SSEN Transmission and National Grid Electricity
Transmission (NGET). The licence permits the installation and operation
of the project's infrastructure in Scottish waters.
The approval follows years of project development, marine surveys, public
engagement and environmental assessments, providing greater insight into
the habitats and species along the planned cable route.
This process has helped shape the planning and design of the project, ensuring
environmental impacts are minimised.
EGL3 will deliver a high-voltage subsea electricity link capable of transporting
renewable energy between Scotland and England, helping to meet growing
electricity demand.
James Johnson, Joint Venture Programme Director at SSEN Transmission, said:
"This marks a really significant moment for the project and reflects
many years of design development and marine survey activities that have
underpinned this successful outcome."
"Throughout the development process, we have worked closely with local
communities, marine stakeholders, offshore developers and asset owners,
whose feedback has helped shape our plans and minimise potential impacts
wherever possible."

title: Wergeland CEO discusses Norway’s offshore wind opportunities
content:
In the latest episode of Offshore Wind Leaders, host Ivar Slengesol spoke
with Margunn Bjørnestad, CEO of Wergeland Group, about leadership, industrial
development and the challenges of building a competitive offshore wind
industry.
Drawing on a career spanning finance, infrastructure and offshore energy,
the conversation examined how offshore wind can benefit from lessons learned
in oil and gas, while recognising the need for a simpler, lower-cost approach.
The conversation explored Wergeland Group's involvement in projects such
as Hywind Tampen, Hywind
Scotland
and Culzean,
and how experience gained through offshore project delivery has helped
shape the company's approach to floating wind.
The episode also examined the challenge of reducing costs, with the view
that floating wind must move beyond demonstration projects and adopt a
more industrialised approach if it is to become more competitive.
Another theme was the need for greater project certainty. Without a steady
pipeline of projects, the industry risks losing talent and investment to
more active markets.
The conversation also highlighted the role of a strong domestic market
in helping Norway build expertise, strengthen its supply chain and compete
internationally.
Workforce development was another area of focus, with discussions over
the need to support the industry's long-term growth, highlighting the importance
of attracting young people to offshore wind and ensuring the sector develops
the leadership required for growth.
The full conversation is available in the fourth episode of Offshore Wind
Leaders, a PowerPod series exploring the people, strategies and decisions
shaping the future of offshore wind.

title: Nexans completes testing milestone for Orkney Link subsea cable
content:
Nexans has reached a milestone for the Orkney Link Project by completing
the Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) of the 220 kV subsea cable connection
between Orkney and mainland Scotland.
The testing concludes more than a year of manufacturing work at the company's
cable facility in Halden, Norway. Successful completion of the FAT confirms
the cable is ready to move into the next stages of project delivery.
The Orkney Link, being developed by SSEN Transmission, it plans to connect
Finstown in Orkney with Dounreay in Caithness through a 220 kV HVAC link.
The project includes approximately 53km of subsea cable and will provide
transmission capacity of up to 220MW.
The new connection is expected to strengthen the electricity network and
support the integration of renewable energy generated in Orkney.
Onshore cable installation and jointing works are expected to continue,
while preparations are advancing for the offshore installation campaign
planned for 2027.

title: Jensen Huang Is Out; Are Inference Providers Screwed?
content: What a week. Jensen Huang , the CEO and cofounder of the world’s second-most-valuable company, resigned, Nvidia said Thursday morning , after reports of extramarital affairs both with a woman alleged to have spied for Beijing as well as a woman who reported to him at Nvidia . Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress will become interim CEO, the company said, while it searches for a permanent successor. Much remains uncertain, including implications for Nvidia’s business of selling advanced AI chips and for Nvidia’s aggressive investments in AI model developers and infrastructure startups that are holding up the AI economy. I’m sure we’ll be getting into all of it in the upcoming days. Meanwhile… It’s not only a tough week to be Huang, but it’s also a tough week to be an inference provider , a well-funded category of startups that help developers use open-source models at high speeds across Nvidia servers. Most recently, Fireworks , one of the most heavily-funded startups in this category, suffered a security breach that exposed customer data to hackers and has also prompted some large customers to consider ditching the service. (In a note to customers, Notion , one of Fireworks’ customers, suggested that, although the inference provider promised it was using zero data retention , meaning that it wouldn’t store any data from Notion after processing a request, Notion later learned that data was actually being retained.) While that incident was bad enough on its own, it exposes a potential systemic vulnerability for the rest of the inference market: the cloud firms that inference providers lease capacity from And that makes me wonder whether it will have a chilling effect beyond Fireworks. The breach was caused by weak security measures at a small cloud provider that Fireworks uses, we reported Wednesday . And increasingly, inference providers are turning to these smaller cloud providers because they can’t rent enough servers from the major cloud providers, such as Microsoft , Amazon and Google , Cathy and I reported in the same article. Capacity shortages have gotten so dire that inference providers like Modal have started using more than 30 different small clouds to access servers they can turn around and rent to their own customers. Many of these cloud providers are young startups themselves and don’t have the security expertise of a major cloud provider. So you can imagine that the sort of breach Fireworks suffered might not be out of the realm of possibility for its competitors, including Baseten , Modal and Fal . Already, I’ve heard of at least one customer of these inference providers that is considering moving its business off these startups. If it did that, it would run open-source models either in its own data centers or with the hyperscalers because its leaders are so spooked about what happened with Fireworks. I’d imagine that other developers, especially those that were affected by the Fireworks breach, would be wary of using alternative inference providers that are sourcing their compute from the same small neoclouds as well. These security concerns could further accelerate the trend Cathy and I wrote about on Wednesday where inference providers buy their own Nvidia servers and stand them up in data centers themselves, rather than renting such servers from other clouds. In building their own data centers, the inference firms could get more control of the security of the cloud services they provide and also improve their gross profit margins, since they’re not paying to rent servers from cloud providers that themselves need to hit certain profit margins. (Margins have been a hurdle for inference providers since they first emerged on the scene three years ago.) This buy-versus-rent approach has its own downsides, though. Finding the power, land and chips to build a data center or even just leasing an existing data center requires a lot of specialized expertise that most companies don’t have. That could explain why inference providers like Fal have job postings for staff to help with data center efforts. And it’s not clear whether the inference providers can do a better job at sourcing chips and managing data centers than the dozens of other cloud providers that are already doing so. Plus doing so requires billions of dollars at a time when the capital markets are seizing up for smaller borrowers (see: the recent neocloud crisis). That’s why Fireworks, for example, has explicitly told investors that it believes acquiring chips and building data centers is a commodity and that its true defensible moat lies in developing software that can run models quickly. Of course, dozens of other firms are trying to do the same thing. Here’s what else is going on… People On The Move Meta Platforms is changing the leadership of its massive data-center operation, with longtime executive Santosh Janardhan telling employees that he is stepping down as head of global infrastructure and will leave the company early next year. Dave Brown , a veteran of Amazon Web Services whom Meta hired in July, will take over as infrastructure head. Big Number Anthropic 's IPO roadshow drew orders for multiple times the 825 million shares on offer within its first day or two on the road, demand that has been credited with helping fuel a broader rally in AI-related stocks, according to Bloomberg. Torus , which builds modular shipping container–sized AI datacenters, raised $500 million in growth capital led by Magnetar. Edelbyte , which built a data platform for AI agents, emerged from stealth with $70 million in total funding, combining a $25 million seed round led by Sequoia Capital , and a $45 million Series A funding round led by Quiet Capital. Bay , a Tel Aviv-based startup that offers AI agent security software, raised $50 million across seed and Series A rounds. Battery Ventures led the $37 million Series A and YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners led the $13 million seed round. Operand , a New York-based startup that offers AI-powered due diligence software for private equity firms, raised $31 million across seed and Series A funding led by Khosla Ventures . Nebuly , which measures the ROI of enterprise AI agents, raised $21 million in Series A funding led by Planven. XpertDox , which uses AI to code medical bills, raised $20 million in Series A funding led by Savant Growth. title: Alice Huang’s Companies Invested in DeepSeek, Promising Nvidia Chips
content: The network of companies tied to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy in a romantic relationship with Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang, recently invested in Chinese AI star DeepSeek, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter. The investments were meant to forge closer ties with DeepSeek so Alice Huang’s companies could supply a steady stream of Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips, which are banned from sale to China, according to one of the three people. The investments, which haven’t previously been reported, illustrate the hidden yet important role Alice Huang and her companies have played in China’s AI industry. DeepSeek shot to global stardom in early 2025, after its R1 model showed capabilities comparable to those of OpenAI’s latest model at the time but was trained at a fraction of the cost. Nvidia’s Huang, whose resignation as CEO was announced on Thursday morning, had been one of DeepSeek’s most prominent admirers. In his keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in January, he said DeepSeek’s R1 was “really, really exciting work.” “We’re so happy with it,” he added. But DeepSeek, like other Chinese AI firms, has been held back by a persistent AI chip shortage, resulting from U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips in place since late 2022. While DeepSeek has been at the forefront of adapting to Huawei chips, it is still trying to gain access to more Blackwell chips, which can be used for research, and as a fallback in case Huawei chips don’t work. During DeepSeek’s second funding round between July and October, DeepSeek employees introduced companies connected to Alice Huang and her family, Century Litong and its parent company, Shanghai-listed Jiangsu Lettall Electronics, to several investors, the people said. The DeepSeek employees made clear that Century Litong and Lettall, collectively referred to as “Litong Inc” in the industry, were a substantial supplier of blackmarket Nvidia AI chips, and therefore deserved allocation in the hotly contested funding round, the people added. Litong Inc. ended up participating in the funding round, which raised 105.5 billion yuan ($15.8 billion) in October, the people said. The companies invested through special purpose vehicles set up by DeepSeek’s investors for the funding round. As a result, no entity from Litong Inc appears directly on DeepSeek’s shareholder list . One of the investments went through a special purpose vehicle set up by Beijing-based venture capital firm Monolith Management, according to stock exchange filings and Chinese corporate records. Lettall invested 95 million yuan ($14 million) in the entity, the records show. Monolith, founded by former Sequoia Capital China partner Cao Xi, is the third-largest investor in DeepSeek after two rounds of funding. It couldn’t be learned how much money in total Litong Inc put in DeepSeek, but a person with direct knowledge of DeepSeek’s second funding round said the group of companies invested through multiple vehicles. Century Litong has priority access to Nvidia’s chips thanks to its status as one of the chip designer’s preferred cloud partners, which it attained just four months after it was founded in 2023. The company operates data centers and rents out AI chips including Nvidia’s graphics processing units. Litong imported 240,000 Nvidia chips worth at least $7.5 billion into China since 2023, despite tightening U.S. export controls, The Information reported earlier this week. The close ties between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang made the imports possible, The Information reported. Century Litong has managed to import Blackwell chips despite a U.S. crackdown on chip smuggling since late last year, according to two other people with direct knowledge of the situation. Alice Huang never held a stake or an executive position at Century Litong or Lettall (whose name in Mandarin is also Litong). The Information mapped out her relationship with these companies through a myriad of former ownerships and corporate transactions that involved her sister Huang Yu and her husband Kang Wei. DeepSeek’s second funding round drew nearly 30 investors, many of them Chinese tech giants and state-affiliated firms. It was the biggest Chinese AI company fundraising so far. The round valued DeepSeek at about 615.5 billion yuan ($92 billion). Tencent and battery giant CATL were the biggest backers.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns, Creating Uncertainty for the AI Sector
content: Nvidia CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resigned in a stunning turn of events that upends the world’s second-most-valuable company and rattles one of the foundations of the AI economy. Finance chief Colette Kress will become interim CEO, Nvidia said in a statement on Thursday morning. The move came three days after the board announced an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.” U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly concluded earlier this year that Huang had developed a close relationship with a woman they believed was spying for Beijing. Huang on Sunday also apologized to Nvidia employees for having an extramarital affair. The company said it was initiating a search for a permanent CEO “and will consider internal and external candidates.” Huang has internally and externally pushed back on the need for a succession plan, according to employees and Huang’s public commentary. He has dozens of direct reports but no clear No. 2. Nvidia’s shares were trading down 12% in early trading on Thursday. In its statement, Nvidia said thanked Huang for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” It did not elaborate on the reasons for Huang’s departure. Nvidia said one of its directors, Harvey Jones, would become the company’s “first-ever chair of the board.” In a securities filing, Nvidia said the board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. His departure appeared to come quickly. As of Tuesday, Huang was operating normally within Nvidia, including preparing for next week’s quarterly earnings call, according to a person familiar with the situation. A Tuesday meeting with Nvidia’s executive staff—a group of 50 or so executives who mostly report directly to Huang—proceeded normally, other than Huang’s delivery of a short apology to his colleagues at the start of the meeting, that person said. But Huang faced other revelations that added to precariousness of his position at Nvidia. Several former employees told The Information that Huang was widely believed to have been in a separate relationship with Kimberly Powell, a vice president who ran healthcare technology-related initiatives at the company and reported directly to Huang. The alleged relationship was widely discussed by employees for years, these people said. Earlier Wednesday, The New York Times earlier reported that video evidence of the affair between the two executives had surfaced internally earlier this year. Huang and Powell, along with representatives for Nvidia and Huang, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Earlier in the week, Nvidia had hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the investigation into Huang’s conduct, and President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating Huang’s relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang. The Information reported Tuesday that Alice Huang worked at a Chinese firm that distributed hundreds of thousands of advanced Nvidia AI chips despite a U.S. ban on their sale to China. Huang’s firing is a major blow to a company that he has become synonymous with since he co-founded it in 1993. Nvidia has soared to Olympian heights during the current AI boom, in part through Huang’s relentless style of leadership and aggressive efforts to stay ahead of its competition. Nvidia’s graphics processing units are the dominant chips for training and running AI models, turning the company into a business juggernaut that reported $216 billion in revenue last year. In recent years, Huang told some senior colleagues that he planned to run Nvidia until he is 120 years old, according to a former Nvidia manager who heard the comments (Huang is currently 63). “This company was built around him for 30 years,” this person said. “This is unimaginable.” Huang’s ouster also creates uncertainty for the broader AI sector. He has been one of the most high-profile public advocates for AI, rebutting concerns about its safety even as others in the industry have raised them. And he has aggressively pumped Nvidia’s cash into a new crop of cloud companies that rent out its server chips to AI developers, as well as into AI developers such as OpenAI. Nvidia is planning to invest $10 billion in Anthropic’s initial public offering next week and has discussed providing credit guarantees related to a proposed data center in West Virginia that Anthropic plans to lease. As of earlier in the fall, Nvidia had $100 billion in equity investments in other companies. Huang’s ouster is likely to rattle stock market investors who have already been skittish about some of the smaller firms that depend on Nvidia server chips and capital to run their businesses. Huang’s successor will likely face questions about whether they plan to continue Nvidia’s practice of investing so freely in its customers. It also remains unclear whether any successor to Huang will have the clout to continue the tactics that helped make Nvidia so dominant—for example, its muscling of key partners like the chip manufacturer TSMC for capacity. The company is facing an array of competitors eager to chip away at its power. Google, AMD and Amazon offer competing server chips, and more potential competition is coming from Anthropic and OpenAI. “Jensen is so singular,” says an executive at a company that is a major customer of Nvidia’s chips. The fallout from Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang could spread beyond him. In recent days, The Information and other media organizations have reported on the reluctance of leaders in the Commerce Department in the past to impose export controls on AI chips and related technologies that would prevent China from getting access to them. Nvidia has lobbied aggressively against such rules in the past. (Late Wednesday, The Information reported that the Commerce Department is finalizing a new rule that would close a loophole that has allowed Chinese AI firms to remotely access advanced AI chips.) Lawmakers from both parties have begun calling for tougher export controls on Nvidia’s chips and related products, which Congress could pass in the coming weeks as part of a collection of legislation called the National Defense Authorization Act. A House subcommittee has also asked Huang to testify behind closed doors at a hearing in Washington next week about his relationship with Alice Huang. The outcome of that and other related probes could lead to further departures from Nvidia. Huang’s ouster could also be awkward for members of his family: His daughter and son, Madison and Spencer Huang , both work at Nvidia, along with Madison’s husband, Nico Caprez .

title: Exclusive: SES AI CEO Says Drone Sales Could Lead to Profit
content: In 2021, SES AI CEO Qichao Hu proudly appeared in a company video brandishing a technological breakthrough: a full-size next-generation lithium-metal battery ready to power an electric vehicle, produced in the company’s new factory in South Korea. But in the five years since then, Hu has found no EV maker prepared to deploy that battery in a commercial car, putting millions of dollars of SES’ investment at risk. So this year, Hu threw in the towel and completely rebuilt the South Korean manufacturing line. Now it’s configured to make batteries one-tenth the size of the EV battery—the perfect scale to power drones. And though SES lost $73 million last year, Hu thinks drone battery sales could eventually allow the company to turn a profit. The pivot reflects the impact of the drone boom on the next-generation battery industry after a roughly four-year-long industry slump. In recent months, startups that had earned either very little or no revenue ever have started to see some real money flow in. Virtually all of the next-gen startups, like SES, continue to lose money. But Hu said the early drone revenue received so far means SES is finally earning some money back on the more than $55 million in accumulated equipment and other capital costs incurred since he founded the company in 2012. “All the technology that we’ve developed the last 14, 15 years, now we are monetizing all that technology,” he told me. It’s the latest abrupt strategic turn for SES, which Hu founded out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he was a postdoctoral researcher. The original idea was to develop a battery that used lithium metal as the anode. The industry as a whole had been seeking to develop such a battery since the 1970s because pure lithium metal delivers exceptional energy density, which would translate into extraordinary EV driving range. But no one could manage that feat because lithium metal can explode or catch fire when it comes into contact with air or moisture. Over the subsequent years, Hu developed various working versions of the battery. In 2016, his lab produced a design known as anodeless, because it created its own lithium-metal anode internally on the first charging cycle, thus not requiring some costly equipment. It delivered energy density exceeding 500 watt-hours per kilogram, well over twice that of conventional lithium-ion batteries. But it would sustain only 10 or so charge-discharge cycles. “We were like, ‘OK, who’s going to want these things?’ No car company would want that. So we just basically filed a patent and then shelved it,” Hu said. Hu went on with development until his big 2021 unveiling of the full-size battery. Honda, Hyundai and General Motors all invested in the company, with loose plans to use the battery in future EVs. Then came the downturn in U.S. EV sales. Suddenly, expensive next-gen batteries no longer interested major car companies, which instead began looking to power their EVs with cheaper “good enough” conventional batteries. All three carmakers ended their battery development projects with SES. To survive, Hu repeatedly changed his plans: He moved SES into stationary storage batteries; he developed a materials discovery system using AI; he added silicon and lithium-iron-phosphate batteries to SES’ repertoire. Those gave SES some cash—last year, the company generated $21 million in revenue, and it projects $30 million to $35 million in revenue this year, most of it from stationary storage batteries. But Hu is now focusing on the drone boom, triggered by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which has taken that anodeless battery off the shelf and into use for interceptor drones. “Drones have thrown a lifeline to a lot of the battery startups in the U.S.,” he said. Last month, SES finished the first stage of reconfiguring the drone battery production line in its Chungju, South Korea, factory. It has the capacity to produce 1 million battery cells per year, enough to power approximately 150,000 small quadcopters. Hu said the company will triple the capacity in the second quarter of next year to 3 million battery cells. He said he is responding to a “flood of orders,” but these are still only from countries and companies validating the performance of SES’ batteries. He said he is on the verge of getting commercial production orders that will take up most or all of the planned production. Compared with the EV market, selling drone batteries is easy, Hu suggested. Car companies spend five or more years putting new batteries through tests before making any commercial production commitment—and so far, virtually no next-gen battery startup has gotten past this gauntlet. “Drones are way faster. It’s maybe nine months of validation,” he said. “For some of the smaller drone companies, it could be like three months or just a week.” Most battery startups I speak with have also pivoted to supplying the drone industry, and I asked Hu whether the market for drone batteries is getting saturated. He said it isn’t. “The drone market is still quite early and still evolving, whether it’s defense or civilian commercial applications,” he said. “I do think battery companies need to move quickly and establish some level of scale to actually matter in the space.”

title: Commerce Department Finalizing Long-Awaited AI Remote Access Rule
content: The Commerce Department is finalizing a long-awaited rule that will prevent Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries, according to two people familiar with the process. The move could help the department push back on criticism that it has acted too slowly to create policies to limit China’s access to advanced AI technologies—rules that have been opposed by influential companies such as Nvidia. The rule, which could be announced as soon as this month, will expand existing semiconductor-related controls from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and extend them to seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to prevent remote access and chip smuggling into China, the people said. Commerce is currently consulting with other government agencies on the rule before it can be finalized, they added. The change will implement a policy that Nvidia has pushed against in previous lobbying efforts, as it would put more stringent requirements on data centers abroad that are major buyers of its chips. Commerce’s decision to finalize the rule could, in part, reflect Nvidia’s waning influence in Washington. Nvidia’s board has been investigating CEO Jensen Huang for an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and is reportedly considering whether to remove Huang from his position. The Bureau of Industry and Security has faced growing criticism that it has moved too slowly in implementing new export control policies at a time of heightened AI competition with China. The remote access loophole, in particular, meant restrictions on chip exports to China could be easily circumvented, allowing Chinese AI companies to train their models using the most advanced U.S. chips. That criticism of the Bureau of Industry and Security and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler has heightened in recent days after news reports that the Commerce Department halted an investigation into Megaspeed, a Singaporean company embroiled in a scandal involving its former top executive and Huang, after Nvidia intervened . Several prominent Republican lawmakers have called for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to explain why the agency has not moved to block Megaspeed from buying advanced chips. The so-called remote access loophole has long been a focus area for export control policy experts, who argue that it allows Chinese AI companies to gain access, through data centers largely in Southeast Asia, to advanced chips that would otherwise be restricted. There have been previous efforts under the Trump administration to address the loophole through Commerce rules, The Information has reported . And the White House recently provided feedback to Congressional staff requesting a provision be added to export control measures currently being debated in a must-pass defense bill that would have required the Commerce Department to create a rule preventing remote access to certain chips, The Information reported Monday. If finalized, the new Commerce rule could allay some of these concerns by taking action on an issue at the top of the wish list for many China hawks. Remote Access Under the current Commerce Department regime, certain countries such as Saudi Arabia and Vietnam need licenses to receive exports of advanced AI chips. The licenses include controls and conditions such as restricting remote access to companies, as well as different security measures that prevent chip smuggling. Along with Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, the new countries that will now be subject to those licensing requirements include Brazil, Indonesia, Norway and South Africa, said the two people familiar with the rule, which extends to Nvidia Blackwell chips and above. One of the people said that in addition to preventing remote access to advanced AI chips, bringing those new countries under the licensing regime could also combat smuggling. That’s because the rule will now require customers seeking chip exports to tell the Commerce Department who is receiving the chips and what they’re going to be used for, and will subject them to ongoing monitoring. The rule will likely face pushback from governments in those countries, as well as U.S. companies who operate there. Under the new rule, however, U.S. company-run data centers in those countries will not require licenses to receive exports of chips, as long as they restrict remote access of AI chips of a certain capability to countries where the U.S. has arms embargos, such as China, Russia and Venezuela. Those U.S. companies will instead be subject to new reporting requirements, including informing the Commerce Department if they have any customers from arms-controlled countries. The companies will also have to report who the customers in those countries are and how much compute they have, one of the people said. While the new rule is restricted to seven additional countries for now, it could expand, according to one of the people, who said the rule is designed to put other countries on notice that chip smuggling and remote access in a way that is contrary to U.S. interests will not be tolerated. The Commerce Department is also planning to formally rescind the Biden-era AI licensing framework known as the diffusion rule, one of the people said. In May 2025, the Trump administration announced its intention to rescind the rule and issue a replacement, though it never formally scrapped it.

title: Nvidia CEO’s Exit Looms
content: Well, that didn’t take long. Jensen Huang’s time as CEO of Nvidia appears to be coming to an end, according to multiple reports that the board was meeting Wednesday night to consider his future. Just three days ago, it announced an inquiry into whether he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” but at the time the board said it had “confidence in Jensen.” It seems likely that confidence was undermined by a New York Times story on Wednesday that said Huang had had an affair with a company executive in addition to an industry executive who may also be a Chinese spy. If the board dumps Huang, it will demonstrate that no CEO is indispensable, no matter how vital their role is. Many observers had insisted the opposite in recent days, perhaps understandably. After all, Huang co-founded the company and still owned 3.6% of the stock, making him one of the biggest shareholders. As we wrote in this piece , he “has a hand in nearly every aspect of the company’s day-to-day operations.” Along with Sam Altman, he’s been probably the most articulate advocate for AI. Most importantly, his vision of the future has positioned Nvidia to benefit more than any other company from the AI boom, driving its market capitalization to a high of $5.8 trillion in early October, according to Koyfin. Not surprisingly, investors have freaked out about the possibility of his exit. After falling 10% in the first two days of this week, Nvidia was trading down 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday to around $160, giving the company a market capitalization of around $3.85 trillion. The question now is who will replace him. There are no obvious internal candidates, although Nvidia could appoint an executive as interim chief. That suggests the board will have to go outside Nvidia. Earlier this week we suggested that either AMD CEO Lisa Su or Arm CEO Rene Haas could succeed Huang. On TITV on Tuesday , D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria suggested Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan. This is a big job. Who can do it? Anthropic’s Not-So-Powerful Trust Anthropic executives are meeting with investors this week, ahead of next week’s expected IPO. Here’s one thing investors should ask: How concerned should they be about the Long-Term Benefit Trust, a secretive group that has the power to appoint and remove a majority of Anthropic’s board? Their job is to ensure the company is run in a way that balances the financial interests of shareholders with Anthropic’s mission to develop advanced AI “for the long-term benefit of humanity.” What a balancing act! And who controls the trust? It turns out that the trustees—who include a former Fed chair, a health policy wonk, and a physics professor at Harvard University—pick future trustees. (There’s a vacancy for a fifth trustee, by the way, and it pays $400,000 a year!) In other words, it’s a closed club, which seems to give those four an extraordinary amount of power. But things are not exactly what they seem. A big restriction on the trust’s power essentially defangs it. The trust appoints and can in theory remove four of Anthropic’s seven directors. In reality, it can only remove three of those four unilaterally. A committee of Anthropic’s board, which includes Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, has to approve the trust’s removal of the fourth board member. If the board committee opposes the director’s removal, Anthropic’s employees get involved and have to approve it. As Amodei and other company co-founders essentially pick three of the seven board members, the co-founders could counter any effort by the trust to replace a majority of the board. The board committee also has a role if the trustees want to remove one of their members. Anthropic says in its filing that “these procedural requirements are intended to promote collaboration between the Trustees and our leadership in identifying and sourcing candidates” for the board and the trust. The rules “do not give our board of directors the substantive ability to limit the LTBT’s freedom to elect directors of its choosing.” It’s hard to take that statement seriously, given that it’s precisely what the requirements do. The point is that it’s the founders rather than the LTBT who control the company. For investors, that’s probably good news, given how aggressively Anthropic competes—see here and here —and given its success in overtaking OpenAI. Of course, as AI models become more sophisticated and more powerful, a clash over its risks to society seems likely. Don’t be surprised if one day a huge fight breaks out between the trust and the board reminiscent of OpenAI’s 2023 brawl over the short-lived removal of CEO Sam Altman. When that happens, expect the founders to prevail. The Information’s Top 50 If there’s one field every parent should encourage their child to go into, it’s cybersecurity. The spread of AI, with the ability to uncover holes in software that hackers can exploit, is becoming a huge deal. NBC News reported this week that cybersecurity firms were “turning away new clients” because they were overwhelmed! It shouldn’t be surprising, then, that cybersecurity is a hot sector for startups. In our latest installment of The Information 50—our annual list of the most promising startups out there—three of the four most highly valued companies are security startups. Here’s the list. In Other News • Meta Platforms is changing the leadership of its massive data-center operation, with longtime executive Santosh Janardhan telling employees that he is stepping down as head of global infrastructure and will leave the company early next year. • United Airlines said Wednesday it will ban AI agents and assistants from booking its flights, following similar bans by banks and retailers that cited privacy concerns. title: Sequoia Capital to Invest in AI Holding Co. Sequence
content: Sequoia Capital is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Sequence Holding, a one-year-old business that just announced a $7.7 billion insurance acquisition co-led by Michael Dell’s family office, say people familiar with the matter. This will be Sequoia’s second known investment in a new category of holding companies. These aim to buy businesses in established industries such as accounting, insurance and HOA management and then replace or complement some human work with AI. The new money raised from Sequoia is likely to allow Sequence, which has been scouting for targets, to make more acquisitions, according to people familiar with the matter. Previously Sequoia invested in its partner Ravi Gupta’s Ithaca Holdings, which announced a $1.3 billion deal to buy dating app Bumble . The planned investment in Sequence, which hasn’t been reported, comes amid an overhaul at Sequoia since partners Alfred Lin and Pat Grady took the leadership reins at the storied venture firm in November. In recent weeks, the firm has merged its early and growth-stage investing team, shut down its London office to focus on U.S. investments and reworked its so-called evergreen fund that its former leader Roelof Botha created to hold shares in startups after they go public for longer than the firm normally does. Under Lin and Grady, the firm has aggressively pursued AI deals this year after Sequoia sat out some major AI investments during Botha’s leadership. The firm co-led Anthropic’s May funding round at a $965 billion valuation and made dozens of AI-related investments since last November. Representatives for Sequoia and Sequence Holdings declined to comment. Dell Partnership Founded in 2025, Sequence Holdings has raised at least $75 million from 8VC, Lux Capital and Conviction. Last month, it took insurance broker Baldwin Group private in a cash and debt deal co-led by Dell’s family office DFO Management. In recent years, venture capitalists have been pouring money into such permanent holding companies, with the goal that they can help modernize these services or traditional businesses with AI tools. Such investments are likely to generate returns more like private equity, say four times the investments, paling besides venture’s targeted 10X returns. But investors say they should be more predictable and generate another way for VC firms to return cash to their backers. These VC-backed AI holdings companies have all done large acquisitions the past year. Josh Kushner’s Thrive Capital last year set up Thrive Holdings, which raised more than $2 billion in funding from investors including Altimeter, D1 Capital Partners and SoftBank. Last month, that firm agreed to buy 152-year-old home security firm ADT in an all-cash deal worth $15.3 billion including debt. Meanwhile, General Catalyst invested in holding company Long Lake in 2024. Earlier this year, Long Lake took American Express Global Business Travel private for $6.3 billion. Sequence Holding has already made a minority investment in privately held community lender BankSouth. Sequence’s CEO Michael Lee said in a podcast interview with Conviction partner Sarah Guo that AI reduced consumer loan underwriting turnaround times by 94% since March and cut commercial loan underwriting from 30 days to 11 days. Lee also said Sequence is taking a different approach than traditional private equity firms, by focusing on doing one deal per year instead of multiple ones, and allowing its engineers to take part in important decision-making.

title: New Startup Voya Energy Proposes Replacement for Loud Diesel Generators in Data Centers
content: In 2023, Shayle Kann, a venture capitalist with Energy Impact Partners, was mulling a longstanding fixation—how to get rid of the loud and polluting diesel generators used to provide backup power for most AI data centers. He put the question to the head of his technology team: Isn’t there some material rivaling the enormous energy density of hydrocarbons that could do the same job cleanly and quietly? The result was Voya Energy, a Hayward, Calif., startup that promises to replace diesel generators with a novel electrochemical process that converts scrap aluminum into electricity without emissions, toxic waste or noise. In August, Kann’s firm led a $35 million Series A round for Voya at a $113 million valuation. Voya leads a lineup of three energy technology companies that made the 2026 edition of The Information 50 , our list of the most promising tech startups, published Wednesday. The other two are Critical Loop, a Long Beach, Calif., startup that offers fast backup power generation, which we profiled last month after it landed a big deal to power an aerospace facility for Anduril Industries; and Parallax, a San Francisco startup that makes natural gas turbines using 3D-printed technology. All three startups fit neatly into the biggest technology boom in decades, offering ways to power AI data centers. Richard Wang, a battery expert whom Kann recruited to be Voya’s CEO, said he expects to deploy pilot versions of the aluminum generator in 2028 and to deliver commercial models to AI data centers and other customers in 2029. But for now, the idea is little more than a concept: No one appears to have ever used metals as fuel to power a commercial industrial facility, and Voya has made only a rudimentary version of the equipment necessary to do so. The idea is that a machine turns scrap aluminum like soda cans into small pellets. A mechanical system loads those pellets into a generator and combines them with an electrolyte, which releases electricity held electrochemically inside the aluminum. The generator delivers that electricity to the data center, and the spent aluminum converts to aluminum trihydrate, which can be used to remake pellets, according to Wang. Voya’s origins start with Kann and his Energy Impact colleague. By early 2024, they had stumbled across a concept that had been around awhile—that the electricity stored in some metals could efficiently deliver a lot of power, just as fossil fuels do. They decided to try to fund a startup to see if they could make that idea work as a business. In 2024, a friend introduced Kann to Wang, a next-generation battery expert. Wang attracted attention in 2021 when he sold Cuberg, a lithium-metal battery startup he co-founded a few years earlier while a graduate student at Stanford University, to Northvolt for an undisclosed amount. Early in 2024, Northvolt shut down Cuberg (and a few months later Northvolt declared bankruptcy). Wang was now out of work. A friend introduced him to Kann, who told him about his idea of how to replace diesel generators. Wang wasn’t impressed. “This looks half-baked,” Wang recalled responding. “I don’t think this is ready to be a company yet, honestly, and I don’t know if I’m the right person to do this right now.” But Wang agreed to join Energy Impact as a technology fellow and explore the concept. After four or so months, he had warmed to the idea. “You look at the ease of producing the metal, the ease of consuming the metal to make electricity, how easy it is to convert it back and forth between metal and metal oxide,” he told me. Wang had started with the periodic table and narrowed down the metals that would be best as electricity generators to magnesium, zinc, iron and aluminum. Aluminum quickly won the bake-off. “Aluminum stands out naturally as having the highest energy density, being an incredibly abundant, very available commodity resource,” he said. Wang told Kann he had changed his mind. “He came to us and he was like, ‘I think this should be a company and I would like to run it,’” Kann said. In April 2025, Energy Impact led a $13 million seed round for Voya. The standard system Wang has in mind would involve two storage containers, one a standard 20-foot-long container with a 2-megawatt aluminum generator, and the other a 10-foot one containing enough aluminum pellets to produce 100 megawatt-hours of energy. Wang said the advantages of such a system include that aluminum rivals hydrocarbons in terms of energy density and can be stored at an industrial site in a much more compact space than diesel because it’s not flammable and releases no emissions. Voya claims the system converts 57% of the pellets into electricity, higher than diesel’s average 35% conversion efficiency. The one ultrapolluting aspect of using aluminum is the smelting stage. By relying on scrap aluminum, Voya is initially avoiding dealing with the smelting question. But Wang said there are ways to sharply reduce the amount of energy used to smelt the metal and the emissions released in the process. “Our ultimate ambition is to really think about designing our own smelting cells and systems and ultimately plants that are of our own creation, because we think that’s the pathway to get to the lowest-cost-possible aluminum,” Wang said.

title: AI Inference Startups Are Quietly Buying Their Own Chips
content: The fast-growing crop of startups that lease computing capacity from cloud firms and then resell it, without spending a nickel on their own AI chips, are at a crossroads. Finding it harder to line up enough computing capacity to serve their customers, some are starting to buy their own chips, which is likely to drastically change the economics of their business. The difficulty in getting enough compute also has pushed some of these startups to look for computational resources from dozens of smaller neoclouds, which tend to have more available capacity than larger hyperscalers such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform. News this week of a hack of Fireworks, one of the best known of these startups, highlights the risk of that approach. The hack was caused by weak security measures at a small cloud used by Fireworks, according to a person with knowledge of the situation. The hack has prompted some of Fireworks’ customers to consider switching to alternative providers. Startups like Fireworks are known as inference providers—because they cater to customers who need chips to run AI models, a process known as inference. They don’t own chips or data centers, instead devoting their efforts to building software that can help customers better optimize running AI models. These firms have grown quickly. Fireworks, for instance, passed $1 billion in annualized revenue in July, the company said, up five times from what it was generating a year earlier, while others like Fal have doubled their revenue pace in a matter of months, The Information reported in September. Fireworks was most recently valued at $17.5 billion, the highest of the group. But the growing difficulty of securing compute could jeopardize the sector’s rapid growth. In some cases, cloud firms are becoming less willing to lease capacity to rivals. CoreWeave earlier this year decided to stop selling compute to Baseten, according to someone with knowledge of the strategy. CoreWeave launched its own inference service in March this year and didn’t want to devote computing resources to a rival, the person said. Someone close to Baseten disputed the idea that Coreweave had reduced the compute it provides to Baseten. A spokesperson for CoreWeave said: “We have good relationships with inference providers and many of them are our partners, consuming CoreWeave services where it makes sense for their business model, which we are happy to support.” Paddy Srinivasan, CEO of cloud firm DigitalOcean, said he prioritizes “customers that have real-end user demand…versus those reselling our capacity…honestly, because we have so much demand from companies that are actually building software on our stack.” DigitalOcean operates its own data center space. Some inference providers have responded by striking deals with a wide range of smaller cloud firms. Modal, for example, went from working with all the major hyperscalers as cloud partners and a few neoclouds in its first four years as a company to signing up to 30 additional neocloud partners in the past year, when it couldn’t get Nvidia Blackwell chips at the prices and quantity it wanted from larger cloud firms, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson in an interview. Modal still works with hyperscalers, though it tends to rent other chips from them, Bernhardsson said. Some cloud industry executives said inference providers that don’t own their own hardware could be left high and dry if demand for computing capacity disappears or bigger firms decide to cut them off. Inference companies are “like the WeWork of the [graphics processing unit] world, where WeWork went out and signed these long-term leases over office space and then turned around and tried to sell it on a short-term basis. It works well while it works, until either demand or financing dries up,” said Kent Draper, chief commercial officer for Iren, which has built its own data centers. “People are seeing the benefits of vertical integration.” No Choice Some inference providers have decided they have no choice but to invest in their own hardware. Fal, which focuses on hosting video and image AI models, has recently started buying its own Nvidia chips to place in leased data centers, said Raghu Rao, who joined Fal in July to help build out its data center strategy. Fal will use the $1.65 billion in venture capital funding it raised earlier this month to help pay for extra compute capacity, including GPU purchases and renting cloud space from AWS. Fal is also hiring staff to help with the data center effort, Rao said. Fal’s plans to buy hardware haven’t previously been reported. “As we’ve grown tremendously, there’s been a need to both lease as well as own our own hardware,” Rao said. Fal has also expressed interest to investors in borrowing money to help it finance hardware purchases, according to a person with knowledge of the plans. Rao declined to comment on the possibility of debt financing. In recent months, inference providers have been talking to lenders and intermediaries about borrowing money to pay for compute contracts with neoclouds, according to someone involved in the deals. The providers are seeking ways to use borrowed money rather than the equity they have raised from venture capitalists to secure the compute they need, the person said. Together, meanwhile, started buying its own hardware last year and was planning to have 250 megawatts of its own data center capacity by the end of 2026, The Information reported in March. Baseten is also looking to buy Nvidia GPUs to place in data centers that Baseten intends to manage, according to people with knowledge of the plans. CoreWeave itself has made a similar transition. Until now, it has mostly operated data centers owned by other companies. But it revealed last year that it is building its own campus, believing that is the best way to control its hardware. Not all inference companies think they need to own hardware, though. Fireworks leaders have told investors the company believes acquiring the physical chips and building and operating data centers is a commodity, and Fireworks has a more defensible moat in building software that can run models quickly, according to ae person familiar with its strategy. It does not currently have plans to buy hardware, another person with knowledge of Fireworks said. Modal has also told investors it’s interested in purchasing more of its own hardware for data centers, a person with knowledge of those plans said. In an interview, Modal CEO Bernhardsson said the company will do whatever it needs to do to get capacity it needs, but he doesn’t think differentiation comes from owning hardware, echoing a critique hardware owners like Iren have lobbed at inference providers such as Modal. “The hardware layer…is not…where I feel like a lot of value is created. At the end of the day, you’re just buying chips and reselling them,” Bernhardsson said. “So we focus on the software layer. That’s where we’re always going to add the most value.”

title: Anthropic’s PE-Backed Venture, Ode, Pushes to Get Paid for AI Results
content: Private equity firms and AI labs are sorting out how to charge clients and hire enough engineers for joint ventures they’ve launched to build custom AI tools for businesses. That comes as private equity firms are looking to the technology to boost profits, including at companies they’ve struggled to sell. One such team-up is Ode with Anthropic , which launched in July with $1.5 billion in capital commitments from investors including Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman. Ode currently charges most of the several dozen businesses it works with a fixed fee to develop and launch custom AI products, people familiar with the partnership say. The company lets clients retain ownership of the AI software it builds, the people said, allowing them to keep using or even sell the tools once completed without paying Ode ongoing fees. Those terms help Ode attract customers that balked at the terms offered by the team of engineers at Anthropic that embeds with enterprises, which seeks to retain ownership of the custom software it builds and license it back to customers, one of the people said. But Ode has been looking at other ways to earn more on AI projects. Some Ode executives initially proposed coinvesting in companies that were also its customers, but Blackstone’s team pushed back on the idea, one of the people said. Instead, Ode decided to charge performance-based bonus fees on top of the fixed project fees, allowing it to earn more if clients hit specific financial targets. Less than 10% of Ode’s clients are paying those performance-based fees, one of the people said, though Ode is aiming to grow that share. Setting the fees can be difficult because the company and its customers both need to agree on how to measure any AI-driven gains, including setting a baseline and financial or product-related goals. The fees may be negotiated once a contract is signed and Ode then does some early exploratory work and collects data, giving both sides enough information to set terms before moving on to the building phase, the people said. Ode inherited some of its business from Fractional AI, a startup founded in 2024 that the venture acquired in May for an undisclosed sum. Fractional already worked mostly with private equity–backed companies to automate tasks and build custom AI software, and Fractional co-founders Chris Taylor and Eddie Siegel became Ode’s CEO and chief technology officer, respectively. One of those clients, risk and compliance software company LogicGate, paid a fixed fee in the low seven figures for a project that began under Fractional last summer and finished this fall, said LogicGate CEO Diego Panama. (LogicGate’s backers include growth equity firm PSG, which led the company’s $113 million funding round in 2021.) Ode engineers built a custom agent that shortened LogicGate’s client onboarding from 120 days to 90 days or less. LogicGate received full intellectual property ownership and training to run the tool independently, Panama said, and it subsequently began selling the agent to other businesses and has signed several deals. The agent is set to launch publicly at the end of the month. Around half of Ode’s clients are software or business services companies, while the rest come from industrial and other sectors. Its client base is split roughly equally between portfolio companies of Ode’s backers, including at least six Blackstone companies, and other businesses. All of the Blackstone portfolio companies working with Ode currently pay fixed fees, including accounting firm Citrin Cooperman, where Ode engineers built a new onboarding system, similar to the work they did at LogicGate. Blackstone typically sets targets to improve earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in a specific division when evaluating how an AI project is working. Other AI services firms are experimenting with similar fee structures. Hyde , backed by Bain Capital Ventures and General Catalyst, launched last year and helps businesses build custom AI models using their own data. Clients then own the customer models and can run them themselves or pay Hyde to host them. Hyde typically assigns two engineers to work with clients for around four weeks per project, charging for that work plus a recurring fee for using its software platform. (Clients also pay for compute based on usage.) Around half its contracted revenue includes a portion of fees tied to results—its fee for an automotive client, for example, is tied to whether agents meet certain car sales goals. Hyde CEO Anirudh Sanga said demand for Hyde’s services has roughly doubled monthly for the past three months. At the same time, a shortage of engineers is limiting how much business AI services firms can take on. Anthropic itself has sought to address the shortage, announcing a $100 million effort last month to train 10,000 deployment engineers at customer and partner companies by the end of next year. Upstart AI services firms are also competing with major tech firms for talent. Microsoft in July committed $2.5 billion to its Microsoft Frontier Co. with the aim of placing 6,000 engineers inside enterprise customers, partnering with consultancies like Accenture and EY . As of November 2025, Fractional had an annual revenue run rate of over $12 million. At the time of the May acquisition, it was generating around $30 million in ARR, which has since nearly tripled, according to people familiar with the matter. But Ode is being selective about the clients it takes on because it doesn’t have enough engineers to handle all potential business, one of the people said, though it has enough demand for at least two to three times its current workload. OpenAI Deployment Co. has faced similar constraints. The venture, backed by TPG and other investment firms including Brookfield Asset Management and Bain Capital, has sought to hire more engineers to expand available capacity. Ode has made several acquihires and acquisitions since launching, including one of Casper Studios , which designed specialized AI products using Claude. Ode remains open to exploring more deals, a person familiar with the venture said, but is looking to expand its services or geographic reach instead of simply adding more people. Hyde, for its part, isn’t currently seeking acquisitions, but it has declined several takeover offers, Sanga said, mostly from large companies looking to quickly establish their own AI deployment team. Fintech and Crypto Startups to Watch Each year, The Information picks 50 startups that have the potential to be breakout stars. This time around, our fintech and crypto category featured new twists on trading and betting and startups positioned to benefit from growth in emerging areas like agentic payments . There’s Fomo, a viral trading app that plans to branch out from memecoins to tokenized stocks, and Catalyst, a startup offering agents that help people trade across venues like prediction markets and crypto exchanges. On the payments side, Natural is offering bank accounts for AI agents, while stablecoin-backed card provider Kast is expanding beyond retail customers by courting merchants. You can view our full 2026 list here , and join our conference call for The Information subscribers at 12pm PT / 3pm ET to discuss the list with several of the founders whose companies are on it. title: The Download: COP31’s climate challenge and the quest for immortality
content:
The Download: COP31’s climate challenge and the quest for immortality
Plus: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists have gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual UN climate talks. But this year’s negotiations are taking place against a particularly tense geopolitical backdrop, as the world falls further behind the Paris Agreement’s goals.
Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action.
Here’s what you need to know about COP31.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Inside the quest for cognitive immortality
Far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going beyond death. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores their ideas, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud.
Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion.
Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang
The board will meet as soon as today to determine his future. (WSJ $)
+ Nvidia’s stock slid 8% after the report was published. (BI)
+ Huang allegedly also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.(NYT $)
+ His exit could send shockwaves across the AI industry. (Axios)
+ Stakes are high in AI's trillion-dollar gamble. (MIT Technology Review)
2 The Nvidia spy scandal is set to tighten chip exports
But Commerce Secretary Lutnick has stalled the curbs. (CNBC)
+ China has signaled it will retaliate if they pass. (FT $)
+ Chinese firms have started stockpiling Nvidia chips. (Reuters $)
+ Democrats appear to be preparing an investigation. (Politico)
3 A startup has built an AI to detect AI-made bioweapons
It runs offline on a laptop with a USB gene sequencer. (Wired $)
+ Ukraine is opening up its battlefield data to train AI weapons. (NYT $)
+ AI is making bioweapons easier to create. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Anduril says its satellite can track spacecraft in orbital night
It uses an infrared sensor to detect hidden satellites. (Ars Technica)
+ Anduril is also making smart glasses for warfare. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Ukraine has reported new restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield
Zelenskyy says they’re hampering drone defenses. (NBC News
6 Even remote Brazilian wildlife has microplastics in its blood
Animals 100 km from waste sites carried them. (Nature)
+ AstroTurf is increasing microplastic levels. (MIT Technology Review)
7 A NASA space camera can spot invasive plants from orbit
It detects how different species’ leaves reflect light. (Economist $)
8 Astronomers have found an “invisible” object that defies stellar theory
It’s likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star. (404 Media)
+ New research has corroborated the first black hole image. (New Scientist $)
+ The search for dark matter has been blown open. (MIT Technology Review)
9 Life may have started with metabolism, not genes
Self-sustaining chemical cycles could have come first. (Quanta)
10 Brain surgery has left a man seeing cat eyes on people
Researchers used AI to render what he sees. (Gizmodo)
Quote of the day
“I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products—are essentially progressive.”
—Alex Karp, Palantir's CEO, tells Politico that he's a devoted Democrat despite recently backing Trump.
One more thing
How Chinese short dramas became AI content machines
China’s short drama industry is fueled by bite-sized, melodramatic, and smutty shows built for smartphone scrolling. Now, many are being made entirely with AI: no actors, camera operators, cinematographers, or CGI specialists required.
An average of 470 AI-generated short dramas were released every day in January. Production timelines have shrunk from months to weeks, while costs have dropped by up to 90%. Storytelling is also increasingly driven by performance data.
The format is rapidly expanding overseas while reshaping the work of writers and production crews. Read the full story on AI’s dramatic impact on China’s short drama industry.
—Caiwei Chen
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Hold your breath watching a skateboarder’s record-breaking 94.3mph run down a Québec hill.

title: Reparieren statt ersetzen: EHLA erneuert hochfeste Fahrwerkskomponenten

Reparieren statt ersetzen: EHLA erneuert hochfeste Fahrwerkskomponenten

Prüfstand für Fahrwerkskomponenten: Hier lassen sich Belastungen untersuchen, wie sie im Betrieb auf sicherheitskritische Bauteile wirken. Besonders beansprucht werden Radachsen, Kolben, Bolzen sowie Kontaktflächen zu Lagern, Buchsen und Dichtungen.
